days.title: MLOps Strategy and the Advantages of Databricks Runtime ML

concepts.heading: What MLOps Manages and Why Stages Are Separate
concepts.body: MLOps is a set of processes and automated steps for managing three kinds of assets: code, data and models. It combines DevOps, DataOps and ModelOps, and its goal is better performance, stability and long-term efficiency of ML systems. These assets move through stages. Early development has loose access limits and little testing, an intermediate stage tests automatically, and the final production stage is tightly controlled. Databricks recommends a separate execution environment for each stage, with clearly defined transitions between them. An execution environment is the place where code creates or consumes models and data: compute, runtimes, libraries and automated jobs. The usual names are development, staging and production, and with Unity Catalog each is normally a catalog such as dev, staging and prod, so privileges differ per stage. The supporting rules are short: keep pipelines and code in Git (Databricks Git folders sync them), keep raw data and feature tables as Delta tables with access controls, track development with MLflow, and manage model versions in Unity Catalog.

concepts.heading: The Recommended Workflow Across the Three Stages
concepts.body: In development, data scientists explore data, build features and train models, logging parameters, metrics and artifacts to MLflow. They ideally get read-only access to the prod catalog so they can compare against production models and data. The output is pipeline code, not a deployed model. On runtimes that still include it, AutoML can speed up this exploration by producing baseline models. In staging, ML engineers run unit tests when a pull request opens, then integration tests that execute the pipelines together in an environment that mirrors production as closely as is reasonable; passing code is merged and a release branch is cut. In production, ML engineers own the pipelines: train on production data, evaluate on held-out data, register the model in Unity Catalog, validate it, and assign the Challenger alias if checks pass. A deployment step compares Challenger with Champion and moves the Champion alias if the new model is better. Batch or streaming jobs load the model by its alias, and monitoring can trigger retraining, which starts as a schedule and later may become alert-triggered.

concepts.heading: Deploy Code, Not Models
concepts.body: Models are created by code, but the two change asynchronously: a fraud model may be retrained weekly with unchanged code, while a large neural network may be retrained rarely and its serving code updated often. In most situations Databricks recommends the deploy code pattern. The training code moves from development to staging to production and the model is trained in each environment, on a subset in staging and on full production data in production. Benefits: the model can be trained on production data even when that data is off limits to development, retraining is safer because the code was reviewed and tested, and supporting code follows the same path. The cost is a steeper hand-off for data scientists. The deploy models pattern copies the trained artifact upward. Consider it when training is very expensive or hard to reproduce, when all work sits in a single workspace, or when there is no external repository or CI/CD process. Its drawbacks are that production data may not be reachable from development and that automated retraining is awkward.

concepts.heading: Advantages of Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning
concepts.body: Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning (Databricks Runtime ML) creates compute with pre-built machine learning and deep learning infrastructure, including the most common ML and DL libraries. You select the Machine learning checkbox in the create compute UI. Databricks marks a subset of libraries as top-tier: they get a faster update cadence, advanced support, testing and embedded optimizations, and are added or removed only in major releases. You do not lose flexibility, because extra libraries can be added as compute-scoped libraries (every notebook on the compute) or as notebook-scoped Python libraries (only that notebook session). The checkbox also sets the access mode to Dedicated, assigned to your account unless you change it, and Unity Catalog data on the ML runtime needs Dedicated mode. Photon can be enabled for Spark SQL, DataFrame and feature engineering work, but it does not speed up Python packages such as XGBoost, PyTorch or TensorFlow. For custom GPU deep learning, current guidance is AI Runtime, a serverless GPU compute offering, instead of Databricks Runtime ML.

examPoints: MLOps manages code, data and models; use separate development, staging and production environments, each normally mapped to its own Unity Catalog catalog.
Databricks recommends deploying code rather than models in most situations; deploy models fits expensive training, a single workspace or no CI/CD.
Databricks Runtime ML supplies pre-built, tested ML libraries (top-tier ones updated faster); the Machine learning option sets Dedicated access mode, and Photon does not speed up XGBoost or PyTorch.

quiz.q: A company trains a model weekly on production data that data scientists are not allowed to read in development. Retraining must be automated and reviewed. Which pattern does Databricks recommend in most situations?
choices: Deploy code: promote the training code through staging and train the model in production
Deploy models: train once in development and copy the artifact to staging and then to production
Train the model manually in production each week and skip the staging environment to save time
Keep one shared workspace and catalog for all stages and separate them only by naming conventions
quiz.explain: Promoting code lets the model be trained on production data in production, and the training code has passed review and integration tests. Copying a development artifact fails when production data is not reachable from development, and a manual or unseparated setup skips the staged controls.

quiz.q: A team creates classic compute with the Machine learning option and then trains an XGBoost model on a pandas DataFrame. Photon is enabled, yet training time does not improve, while their Spark SQL feature pipeline gets faster. What explains this?
choices: Photon applies only to compute that uses the Standard access mode, which the Machine learning option disables
Photon accelerates Spark SQL and DataFrame work but not Python packages such as XGBoost
Databricks Runtime ML replaces the XGBoost library with a slower pure Python version on Photon compute
Photon needs the XGBoost library to be installed as a notebook-scoped library before it can help
quiz.explain: Photon speeds up Spark SQL, DataFrame and feature engineering workloads. Python libraries like XGBoost, PyTorch and TensorFlow run outside its engine, so they see no gain. The access mode and library scope are unrelated to this effect.

days.recap: MLOps moves code, data and models through separate development, staging and production environments, usually one catalog each. Databricks recommends promoting code so the model is retrained in production, and Databricks Runtime ML gives ready, tested ML libraries on Dedicated compute.

days.title: AutoML: Model and Feature Selection and Its Benefits

concepts.heading: How AutoML Finds a Good Model
concepts.body: AutoML simplifies applying machine learning to a dataset by automatically finding the best algorithm and hyperparameter configuration. You supply the table, pick the problem type (classification, regression or forecasting) and the prediction target, and use either the low-code UI or the Python API. AutoML cleans and prepares the data, orchestrates distributed training and tuning across several algorithms, and presents the best model found with evaluation based on scikit-learn, xgboost, LightGBM, Prophet and ARIMA. For classification the algorithms are decision trees, random forests, logistic regression, XGBoost and LightGBM. Regression uses decision trees, random forests, linear regression with stochastic gradient descent, XGBoost and LightGBM. Classic compute forecasting uses Prophet and Auto-ARIMA. The evaluation metric you choose is the primary metric used to score runs. So model selection is the search across algorithms and hyperparameters, and each combination is a trial that is scored on a validation split. AutoML is not a replacement for judging the result: you still check the metric and the data.

concepts.heading: Controlling Features, Imputation and Splits
concepts.body: AutoML does not decide the business meaning of your columns, but it gives you levers over the inputs. You can choose which columns it uses for training, for example dropping an identifier such as customer_id that carries no signal; the prediction target and the time column used to split the data cannot be removed. You can choose how null values are imputed in the Impute with dropdown; by default AutoML selects a method from the column type and content, and a non-default method turns off semantic type detection. You can exclude training frameworks from consideration. For classification and regression you can pick a time column so training, validation and test data are split in chronological order, which avoids training on the future. You can also augment the input table with existing feature tables from Feature Store, joined by key. AutoML incorporates early stopping for classification and regression, stopping when the validation metric stops improving. The data directory field should normally stay empty so the dataset is stored securely as an MLflow artifact.

concepts.heading: Benefits: Glass-Box Notebooks and Tracked Trials
concepts.body: AutoML is a glass box rather than a black box. For each trial it generates a source-code notebook, so you can review, reproduce and modify the code. For forecasting, notebooks for all trials are imported into the workspace automatically. For classification and regression, the data exploration notebook and the best trial notebook are imported; notebooks for other trials are saved as MLflow artifacts of each run and can be imported by hand in the experiment UI or with the databricks.automl.import_notebook API. The data exploration notebook summarizes the dataset, and the same mechanism feeds the MLOps development stage as a baseline. Every trial is an MLflow run with parameters, metrics and the model, so trials can be compared and the best one registered. The generated notebooks contain code for Shapley values (SHAP), which estimate each feature's importance to predictions; because the computation is memory-intensive it is off by default, and you set shap_enabled = True in the feature importance section and re-run. A regulated team can therefore start from AutoML and still show auditors the exact code.

concepts.heading: Requirements and Availability
concepts.body: AutoML depends on the databricks-automl-runtime package, and no libraries other than those preinstalled in Databricks Runtime ML should be installed on the cluster. Removing, upgrading or downgrading an existing library version causes run failures through incompatibility, which is a classic exam trap. Compute access mode matters: Dedicated mode supports both AutoML and Unity Catalog, Standard mode supports Unity Catalog but not AutoML, and No isolation shared supports AutoML but not Unity Catalog. Results are stored in a databricks_automl folder in the home folder of the user who ran the experiment. Availability has changed: AutoML has been removed from Databricks Runtime ML 18.0, so in Databricks Runtime 18.0 ML or above it is not included as a built-in library, although the documentation for it remains. It therefore runs only on earlier ML runtimes. For the exam, treat AutoML as the fast way to get a baseline and tuned candidate models with visible code, and not as a feature selection engine that removes weak columns by itself.

examPoints: AutoML picks the algorithm and hyperparameters by training many trials across algorithms (trees, forests, logistic or linear regression, XGBoost, LightGBM; Prophet and Auto-ARIMA for forecasting) and scoring them with the chosen metric.
You can select training columns, choose the imputation method, exclude frameworks, split by a time column and add feature tables; the target and the split time column cannot be removed.
Benefits: a source-code notebook per trial, a data exploration notebook, MLflow-tracked trials and optional SHAP; changing preinstalled library versions breaks AutoML runs.

quiz.q: A data scientist wants a quick baseline for a churn classifier and must show auditors the exact preprocessing and training code, then edit the best model by hand. Which AutoML capability fits?
choices: Each trial is reported only as a metric, and a registered model is produced without any code
A source-code notebook is generated for the best trial, to review, reproduce and modify
AutoML writes a scheduled pipeline that retrains the model automatically every night
AutoML exports every trial as a Unity Catalog function that cannot be edited afterwards
quiz.explain: AutoML produces editable source-code notebooks for trials, with the data exploration and best trial notebooks imported into the workspace. It is not a black box, and it does not create pipelines or locked functions.

quiz.q: After a pip upgrade of scikit-learn on a Databricks Runtime ML cluster, every AutoML experiment on that cluster fails. What is the most likely cause?
choices: AutoML cannot run on any cluster that has Photon enabled, so the cluster must be recreated
The Prediction target column was removed from the experiment configuration by mistake
The cluster uses Dedicated access mode, which AutoML does not support at all
Changing preinstalled library versions makes them incompatible with AutoML, so runs fail
quiz.explain: AutoML requires the preinstalled library versions, and removing, upgrading or downgrading them causes run failures. Dedicated mode is a supported access mode, and the target column would produce a configuration error rather than a library failure.

days.recap: AutoML trains and tunes many algorithms, scores trials with your metric and gives you editable notebooks, tracked MLflow runs and a data exploration notebook. You control columns, imputation, frameworks and time splits, and you must not alter the preinstalled libraries.

days.title: Feature Tables in Unity Catalog: Benefits, Creating and Writing

concepts.heading: Why Feature Tables and Why Unity Catalog
concepts.body: A feature store is a central place to find and share features, and it makes sure that the code that computes feature values for training is the same code used for inference, removing training-serving mismatches. In Unity Catalog, any Delta table with a primary key constraint can be a feature table. Databricks documentation recommends Feature Views for new use cases, where Databricks computes and manages the pipelines, while feature tables remain the option where you populate the Delta tables yourself. Feature tables in Unity Catalog beat workspace-level ones in several ways. They are governed by Unity Catalog privileges like any other data asset. They are accessible from the workspaces assigned to the table's metastore, subject to privileges, which enables sharing and discovery across workspaces. They record lineage between tables, functions and the models trained from them, viewable in Catalog Explorer. The Workspace Feature Store is deprecated and available only for workspaces created before a cutoff date, so on the exam choose Unity Catalog. The Python client is FeatureEngineeringClient, from the databricks-feature-engineering package, which is preinstalled on ML runtimes.

concepts.heading: Creating a Feature Table
concepts.body: Three routes exist. In SQL, create a Delta table whose entity key columns are NOT NULL and add a primary key constraint, for example CONSTRAINT customer_features_pk PRIMARY KEY (customer_id). With Python, FeatureEngineeringClient.create_table creates the table and can attach tags. Or convert an existing Unity Catalog Delta table: set each key column to NOT NULL with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL, then ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY(...). Only the table owner can declare the primary key constraint, and no copy of the data into a separate feature store is needed. Feature tables use the three-level name catalog.schema.table, so you need privileges such as USE CATALOG and CREATE SCHEMA. For features that change over time, add a time column to the key and mark it with the TIMESERIES keyword, for example PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, ts TIMESERIES). That declaration enables point-in-time lookups later. A simple SELECT view over a single table can act as a feature table, but only for offline training: it cannot be published to an online store.

concepts.heading: Writing Data to a Feature Table
concepts.body: Once the table exists you write to it like any Delta table, and FeatureEngineeringClient.write_table adds feature-aware behavior. With mode merge, rows are matched on the primary key: rows whose key is in the DataFrame are updated or inserted, and rows whose key is absent stay unchanged. That is the right call for a nightly job that recomputes only active customers. To add a new feature, run write_table with a DataFrame that has the primary key and the new column; the schema is updated and the values merge by key. Pass a streaming DataFrame to write_table and it returns a StreamingQuery, so features can stay fresh from a Structured Streaming source. Databricks recommends a scheduled job that runs a notebook calling write_table so values do not go stale. Do not change the primary key, the partition key, or the name or data type of an existing feature, because downstream training and serving pipelines break. Read values back with read_table.

concepts.heading: Keeping History and Choosing the Key
concepts.body: A feature table normally holds one row per key, so overwriting yesterday's value loses history. To store past values of daily features, define a composite primary key that includes the date, such as (date, customer_id), and a partition key on date, or enable liquid clustering on the table for efficient reads, which Databricks recommends. Then filter on date to read the time period of interest. A second approach is a time series feature table, where the time column is declared with TIMESERIES (the timeseries_columns argument in the Python client). With it, create_training_set and score_batch perform an as-of join that returns the latest feature values at or before each row's timestamp, so the model never trains on values from after the label event. If you only designate a time column as a key without the time series declaration, joins match exact timestamps and no point-in-time logic is applied. Use time series tables whenever feature values change over time, for example event data or time-aggregated data. Deleting a feature table also drops the underlying Delta table.

examPoints: Any Unity Catalog Delta table with a primary key constraint is a feature table; convert an existing table by setting key columns NOT NULL and adding the constraint (owner only).
Unity Catalog feature tables bring Unity Catalog governance, cross-workspace access through the metastore and model lineage; the workspace feature store is deprecated.
write_table with mode merge updates rows by key and leaves other keys unchanged; use TIMESERIES keys for point-in-time lookups and never alter keys or existing feature types.

quiz.q: A nightly job recomputes features only for the roughly 5 percent of customers that were active, and rows of all other customers must stay as they are. Which call fits?
choices: Run write_table with mode merge so rows match on the primary key and others stay
Drop the feature table and recreate it from the DataFrame of active customers each night
Write the DataFrame with overwrite mode so the table holds only the active customers
Run create_table again with the active customers so existing rows are replaced by key
quiz.explain: Merge mode matches rows on the primary key, so only the listed keys are updated or inserted. Dropping, overwriting or recreating the table discards the customers that were not recomputed.

quiz.q: A Delta table in Unity Catalog has one row per customer_id and no constraints. A data scientist wants to use it for training with Feature Store. What is required?
choices: Copy the table into the Workspace Feature Store of the notebook's workspace before any use
Convert the table to a materialized view, because only views can be used as feature tables
Create a Feature View first, because existing Delta tables cannot be used for training
The owner sets the key columns NOT NULL and adds a primary key constraint
quiz.explain: A Unity Catalog Delta table becomes a feature table once it has a primary key constraint on NOT NULL key columns, added by the owner. No copy to a separate store is needed, and the workspace store is deprecated.

days.recap: Feature tables are Unity Catalog Delta tables with a primary key, created by SQL, the Python client or an ALTER TABLE on an existing table. Merge writes update by key, TIMESERIES keys enable point-in-time lookups, and keys and feature types must not change.

days.title: Training and Scoring with Feature Tables; Online vs Offline

concepts.heading: Building a Training Set with FeatureLookup
concepts.body: To train with features you describe what to fetch and how to join it. A FeatureLookup names a feature table, the feature_names to take (None takes all non-key columns), and the lookup_key, the column of your training DataFrame that matches the table's primary key. FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set takes the DataFrame with raw rows and labels, the list of lookups, the label column, and optionally exclude_columns. It left-joins each feature table to the DataFrame on the keys, and training_set.load_df() returns the result. When the DataFrame column names differ from the table keys, give lookup_key the DataFrame names in the same order as the table keys. Use output_name to rename a feature when two lookups bring the same name, for example the temperature of a pickup zip and a dropoff zip from the same table, and default_values to fill features for keys that have no row. Drop key columns the model must not see with exclude_columns. A time series table needs timestamp_lookup_key set to the DataFrame's event time column to get an as-of join.

concepts.heading: Logging and Scoring Models That Carry Features
concepts.body: For a model to look up its features by itself, three conditions apply. Train on the DataFrame returned by load_df without changing it; changes you make afterwards, such as scaling, are not part of the feature metadata and are not repeated at inference. Log the model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model and pass the training_set, which stores references to the feature tables in the model. And use a model type with an MLflow Python flavor, such as scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch or Spark ML. A plain mlflow.sklearn.log_model call stores no feature metadata. At inference, score_batch takes the model URI and a DataFrame with only the lookup keys; it joins the features from the offline tables and returns the DataFrame with the feature columns and a prediction column. To override a feature, include a column of that name and only the rest are looked up. A column that came from outside the feature tables, such as a browser column, must always be supplied. MLflow pyfunc can also retrieve features for batch inference, but models that use time series feature tables need score_batch.

concepts.heading: Offline and Online Feature Stores
concepts.body: The offline store is the set of feature tables materialized as Delta tables in Unity Catalog. It serves feature discovery, model training and batch inference, where throughput matters more than milliseconds. The Databricks Online Feature Store, powered by Lakebase, is a low-latency, high-scale store for online applications and real-time models, such as recommendations and fraud detection. You create an online store and then sync a table with publish_table. Prerequisites: a primary key constraint with non-nullable key columns, and Change Data Feed enabled on the offline table for the TRIGGERED (default) and CONTINUOUS publish modes. A table declared with TIMESERIES publishes only the latest value per entity, deduplicating rows that share a key but differ in time, which is the usual case for online serving. A model trained with create_training_set and logged with the feature client can be deployed to Model Serving, which looks up features from the online store by key at request time. Online stores continuously incur costs, so delete unused ones. If predictions are computed overnight for millions of customers, skip the online store and run score_batch on the offline tables.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Path for a Scenario
concepts.body: Match the access pattern to the store. Training: offline Delta tables through create_training_set. A nightly scoring job that produces next-day campaign lists: score_batch against the offline tables, with no endpoint and no online store. A payments app that must score a transaction within a few milliseconds using features that change during the day: publish the feature tables to the online store and serve the model on a Model Serving endpoint, so the caller sends only the key and any real-time inputs. If a value exists only at request time, a FeatureFunction computes on-demand features that combine real-time inputs with stored ones. Predictions that are needed with low latency but can be computed offline can also be generated in batch and then published to an online key-value store such as DynamoDB or Cosmos DB. The recurring trap is paying for an online store when there is no latency requirement, or expecting an offline Delta table to answer single-key requests in milliseconds. Remember also that a feature table backed by a simple SELECT view is offline only.

examPoints: create_training_set left-joins feature tables to your labeled DataFrame through FeatureLookup keys; use output_name for duplicate names, default_values for missing keys and timestamp_lookup_key for point-in-time joins.
Log with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model(training_set=...) and train on the unmodified load_df output; score_batch then needs only keys and returns a prediction column.

Offline Delta tables serve training and batch scoring; the Lakebase-powered online store, filled by publish_table (non-null keys; Change Data Feed for triggered or continuous sync), serves low-latency real-time inference.

quiz.q: A model was trained on training_set.load_df() and then logged with fe.log_model passing the training_set. A nightly job has a DataFrame containing only customer_id and product_id. What does fe.score_batch return?
choices: Only the prediction column, because the feature columns are dropped after scoring
An error, because the batch DataFrame is missing every feature column the model needs
The batch DataFrame with the looked-up feature columns added and a prediction column
The feature tables themselves, joined to the labels used during training
quiz.explain: A model logged with the feature client carries references to its feature tables, so score_batch looks the features up by key and returns the input with the feature columns and a prediction column. No feature columns have to be supplied.

quiz.q: A fraud model must answer a payments app within a few milliseconds using customer features that update all day. Which design fits?
choices: Run score_batch every minute and write the predictions to a Delta table that the app queries
Publish the feature tables to the online store and serve the model with Model Serving
Read the offline feature tables from the application with a SQL warehouse at request time
Train the model again at every request using a fresh create_training_set call
quiz.explain: Real-time, low-latency use needs the online store, which is filled by publish_table, plus a Model Serving endpoint that looks the features up by key. Batch tables and warehouse queries do not meet a millisecond budget.

days.recap: Training sets are built with FeatureLookup and create_training_set, and models logged with the feature client look up features themselves in score_batch. Offline Delta tables cover training and batch scoring, while the Lakebase-powered online store covers real-time serving.

days.title: MLflow: Client API, Manual Logging and the MLflow UI

concepts.heading: Experiments, Runs and Where They Are Logged
concepts.body: MLflow tracking logs notebooks, datasets, parameters, metrics, tags and artifacts. A run is a single execution of model code; an experiment is a collection of related runs. Databricks hosts the tracking server, so no setup is needed, and two settings control where data goes: the tracking URI (default is the current workspace) and the experiment. If you call mlflow.start_run() with no active experiment, runs go to the notebook experiment, which is tied to that notebook and deleted with it. A workspace experiment is not tied to a notebook, and any notebook can log to it with mlflow.set_experiment with the path or the experiment ID, which is how a team collects runs in one place. Autologging, for example for scikit-learn, records parameters, training metrics and the model with almost no code, and it is the easiest start. For more control, such as extra plots or business metrics, use the logging API. With MLflow 3, a model produced by a run is a distinct LoggedModel entity, and the lifecycle of models across training and evaluation runs can be tracked.

concepts.heading: Identifying the Best Run with the Client API
concepts.body: The MLflow Python client search_runs API returns a pandas DataFrame, which you can analyze programmatically; the Read MLflow experiments data source returns a Spark DataFrame instead. A search takes experiment IDs, an optional filter expression, a list of columns to order by, and a maximum number of runs. The REST Search runs API documents the same fields: order_by entries name an attribute, param, metric or tag with an optional ASC or DESC annotation, where ASC is the default, and max_results caps how many runs return. To get the single best run by error, order ascending by the metric and keep one row: mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], order_by=["metrics.rmse ASC"], max_results=1). Order descending for metrics where larger is better, such as accuracy. The filter is a subset of SQL that ANDs comparisons between a param, metric or tag and a constant, for example metrics.rmse < 1 and params.model_class = 'LogisticRegression'. The UI search uses the same metrics., params. and tags. prefixes and adds MIN and MAX over a metric's history. A metric logged per epoch keeps its history, so the best-run question depends on whether you want the last value or the minimum or maximum.

concepts.heading: Logging Manually: Parameters, Metrics, Artifacts and Models
concepts.body: Inside a run you log what you decide: parameters are inputs, metrics are results, and artifacts are output files such as CSV files or plots. Autologging is the easiest start, and the logging API gives more control over which parameters and metrics are logged and which extra artifacts are saved. Metrics can be logged with steps, so a value logged per epoch keeps its history, and the MIN and MAX filters in the UI work on that history. A model is logged with the flavor function for its library, for example mlflow.sklearn.log_model. This saves it in the MLflow Model format, which defines flavors such as python-function, pytorch and sklearn, and MLflow automatically logs requirements.txt and conda.yaml, which recreate the environment. A model logged this way can be loaded, registered and served for batch inference on Spark or through a REST API. Models stored outside MLflow-managed storage or a Unity Catalog volume cannot be registered. With MLflow 3, a model is a LoggedModel with its own metadata, and evaluation metrics can be linked to it through log_metrics with a model ID.

concepts.heading: What the MLflow UI Shows
concepts.body: The experiment details page lists all runs with a Source column linking to the notebook version that created each run. You can filter by expressions such as metrics.r2 > 0.3 AND tags.estimator_name="RandomForestRegressor", by parameter values, by tags (tags.<key>="<value>") and by state, time created or dataset. Metric filters use the last logged value by default, while MIN(metrics.x) and MAX(metrics.x) test the lowest or highest value in the history; only runs logged after August 2024 have these. Selecting two or more runs and clicking Compare shows parameters and metrics in tables, and you can chart results. A run page shows the run ID, parameters, metrics, the source notebook link, tags that you can add or edit, and an Artifacts tab with logged files and the model, with code snippets to load it for Spark and pandas DataFrames. Deleted runs stay recoverable for 30 days through the Deleted state filter. Artifacts stored in a location other than MLflow-managed storage or a Unity Catalog volume, for instance an S3 path, do not show in the UI and their models cannot be registered.

examPoints: A run is one execution of model code and an experiment groups runs; without set_experiment, runs go to the notebook experiment, while a shared workspace experiment collects runs from many notebooks.
mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids, order_by=["metrics.<m> ASC|DESC"], max_results=1) returns the best run as a pandas DataFrame; filters compare metrics., params. or tags. values.

Log parameters, metrics (with steps) and artifacts manually when autologging is not enough; log_model adds the MLflow Model format, requirements.txt and conda.yaml; the UI compares, filters (including MIN and MAX) and restores deleted runs for 30 days.

quiz.q: A team ran 60 tuning trials that each logged a metric named rmse to the experiment with ID 1234. One notebook cell must return only the single run with the lowest rmse as a pandas DataFrame. Which call does this?
choices: mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], order_by=["metrics.rmse DESC"], max_results=1)
mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], order_by=["metrics.rmse ASC"], max_results=1)
mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], filter_string="rmse = MIN")
mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], order_by=["params.rmse ASC"], max_results=60)
quiz.explain: Ordering the metric ascending and taking one row returns the lowest error. Descending order returns the worst run, rmse is a metric rather than a parameter, and MIN is documented only as a function over a metric, as in MIN(metrics.rmse), not as a value in a filter.

quiz.q: A teammate bulk-deleted several runs from an experiment eight days ago by mistake, and the team needs them back. What brings them back?
choices: Nothing can be done, because deleted runs are removed at once and training must be repeated
Re-run the notebook with autologging on, which re-creates the deleted runs from its history
Restore the experiment from the Trash folder, because runs are kept only inside experiments
Show the Deleted state on the experiment page, select the runs and click Restore
quiz.explain: Deleted runs are kept for 30 days. Choosing Deleted in the State field lists them, and Restore returns them to Active. Autologging only logs new runs, and the Trash folder matters for notebook experiments, not for restoring individual runs.

days.recap: MLflow tracks runs in experiments on a hosted server. Use search_runs with an ordered metric to find the best run, log parameters, metrics, artifacts and models manually where autologging is not enough, and use the MLflow UI to filter, compare, inspect and restore runs.

days.title: Registering Models in Unity Catalog and Why It Replaces the Workspace Registry

concepts.heading: Three-Level Names and register_model
concepts.body: Models in Unity Catalog share the namespace of tables, so every registered model has a three-level name `<catalog>.<schema>.<model>`, for example `prod.ml_team.churn_model`. The registered model is a securable object: access control, auditing, lineage and discovery work as they do for other Unity Catalog objects. With MLflow 3 the default registry URI is `databricks-uc`; in an older setup `mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")` points the client at Unity Catalog, otherwise it targets the workspace registry. To register a model that a run already logged, call `mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "prod.ml_team.churn_model")`. It creates the registered model when it does not exist and otherwise adds a new version, numbered by the registry itself. Passing the full three-level name as `registered_model_name` to a `log_model` call logs and registers in one step. The catalog, schema and name describe the environment and its governance rules, such as who may delete, but not whether a version serves traffic. Deployment status is expressed with aliases.

concepts.heading: Privileges, Signatures and Compute
concepts.body: Registration is governed by Unity Catalog privileges. To create a new registered model you need `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema and `CREATE MODEL` (or `CREATE FUNCTION`) on that schema, granted for example with `GRANT CREATE MODEL ON SCHEMA <schema> TO <principal>`. To add a version to an existing model you must own it, or hold `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on it plus the catalog and schema usage privileges. Loading or deploying a model needs `EXECUTE` on it. The compute must have access to Unity Catalog; for ML workloads that means dedicated access mode. Every new version in Unity Catalog needs a model signature, the schema of inputs and outputs. You get one automatically from Databricks autologging, or by passing an `input_example` to `mlflow.<flavor>.log_model`, which lets MLflow infer the signature. A missing signature is a common reason a registration is rejected. To let several people maintain one model, transfer its ownership to a group that includes them, since privileges alone do not share write access to the model itself.

concepts.heading: Unity Catalog Registry versus the Workspace Registry
concepts.body: The Workspace Model Registry is legacy. It lives inside one workspace, organizes versions into stages (None, Staging, Production, Archived) that users move between, and offers webhooks and email notifications. Since April 2024 it is disabled for workspaces in new accounts whose default catalog is in Unity Catalog. Models in Unity Catalog are what Databricks recommends. Access control is centralized, so privileges, auditing and lineage follow the model. Any workspace attached to the same metastore can use a model if the user holds the privileges, so a dev workspace can load the production model as a baseline to compare against a new one. Aliases and tags replace stages, and a model can be shared with other regions or accounts through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing. Environments map to catalogs, so promotion is a copy plus a governed alias change rather than a stage transition. Stage-based questions describe the legacy registry; alias-based answers describe the current one.

concepts.heading: Loading, Copying and Migrating Versions
concepts.body: Once registered, a version is addressed by `models:/prod.ml_team.churn_model/3` or through an alias. Versions can carry descriptions, set with `update_model_version`, and can be deleted with `delete_model_version`, which cannot be undone; both need ownership of the model. To log lineage you can pass the training table to MLflow, so the model page shows which Unity Catalog table fed it. A version can be copied between registered models with the MLflow Client API `copy_model_version`, for example from `staging.ml_team.fraud_detection` to `prod.ml_team.fraud_detection`; it needs `EXECUTE` on the source and ownership of the destination or `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on it, plus usage privileges on both locations, and copying can take time. The same call is the recommended way to migrate versions out of the Workspace Model Registry into Unity Catalog, using MLflow client 3.4.0 or later. Copying avoids retraining when training is expensive, but it moves an artifact, not the code that produced it, which matters for promotion strategy.

examPoints: A question that shows a model name with one or two parts, or a registration that fails for a new model, is testing the `<catalog>.<schema>.<model>` name, the registry URI and the `CREATE MODEL` privilege on the schema.
A question that offers stages, Production transitions or webhooks as the solution is describing the legacy workspace registry; the current answer uses Unity Catalog with aliases and tags.
A question about sharing a model across workspaces, lineage or one governance model for tables and models is testing the benefits of Unity Catalog over the workspace registry.

quiz.q: A data scientist has `USE CATALOG` on `prod` and `USE SCHEMA` on `prod.ml_team`, and her cluster uses dedicated access mode. Calling `mlflow.register_model(uri, "prod.ml_team.churn_model")` for a brand-new model fails with a permission error. Which grant fixes it?
choices: `SELECT` on the schema, because the model reads training tables through the schema while it is registered
`CREATE MODEL VERSION` on the registered model, which grants the right to start and name the model
`CREATE MODEL` on the `prod.ml_team` schema, which permits creating a new registered model there
`APPLY TAG` on the catalog, because registration writes metadata and a tag to the new model
quiz.explain: Creating a registered model is a schema-level right, held with usage on the catalog and schema. A version-level privilege cannot be used before the model exists, reading tables is unrelated, and tags are optional metadata.

quiz.q: A company runs separate dev and prod workspaces on one metastore. Data scientists need to load the production model in dev to compare it with a new candidate, with access control and lineage, and the team wants to mark the serving version without moving it through stages. What should they do?
choices: Register in Unity Catalog under prod, grant the dev group `EXECUTE`, and mark the serving version with an alias
Keep a workspace registry in each workspace and move the Production stage between them with webhooks after every approval
Export model files from prod to dev storage by hand and register a second, independent copy in the dev workspace registry
Register in the dev workspace registry only and ask the prod team to read it through the stage name Production
quiz.explain: Unity Catalog models are reachable from any workspace on the metastore under normal privileges, and aliases replace stages. Separate workspace registries or manual copies lose the shared governance and lineage.

days.recap: Register with `mlflow.register_model(uri, "catalog.schema.model")`; the registry assigns versions. Creating a model needs `CREATE MODEL` on the schema plus usage privileges, and versions need a signature. The workspace registry (stages, webhooks) is legacy; Unity Catalog adds shared governance, lineage, cross-workspace access, aliases and `copy_model_version`.

days.title: Promoting Code or Models, Model Tags and Champion/Challenger Aliases

concepts.heading: Deploy Code versus Deploy Models
concepts.body: Models are made by code, but code and model artifacts change asynchronously: a fraud model may be retrained weekly with unchanged code, while a large network may be trained rarely and its serving code updated often. Databricks recommends deploy code. The training code is developed in dev, moved to staging and then production, and the model is trained in each environment, on a subset in staging for integration tests and on the full data in production. This suits organizations that restrict production data, makes automated retraining safer because the code was reviewed and tested, and lets supporting code follow the same path. Its cost is a steeper learning curve for data scientists. Deploy models promotes the artifact trained in dev after staging tests. Consider it when training is very expensive or hard to reproduce, all work is in one workspace, or there is no external repo or CI/CD. Its weaknesses are blocked access to production data from dev, tricky retraining and separate deployment of supporting code. A hybrid trains in staging on full data, then promotes the model.

concepts.heading: Setting and Removing Model Tags
concepts.body: Tags are key-value pairs on registered models and on model versions, used to label and categorize them by function or status. A model might carry `task:question-answering`, and a version under review `validation_status:pending`, later changed to approved. Setting a tag needs ownership or the `APPLY TAG` privilege on the registered model, plus `USE SCHEMA` and `USE CATALOG`. With the MLflow Client API the calls are `set_registered_model_tag(name, key, value)` and `delete_registered_model_tag(name, key)` for the model, and `set_model_version_tag(name, version, key, value)` and `delete_model_version_tag(name, version, key)` for one version. Tags can also be edited in the UI. A validation pipeline often writes a status tag such as `PENDING`, then `PASSED` or `FAILED`. Tags describe a model; they do not select which version a job loads. A tag is the wrong answer to a question about pointing a workload at the current production version, which is the job of an alias.

concepts.heading: Aliases for Champion and Challenger
concepts.body: A model alias is a mutable, named reference to one version of a registered model; setting or deleting one requires owning the model. A common convention marks the version in production as `Champion` and a version under evaluation as `Challenger`. With the client: `client.set_registered_model_alias("prod.ml_team.iris_model", "Champion", 1)` creates the alias, running it again with version 2 reassigns it, `get_model_version_by_alias` resolves it and `delete_registered_model_alias` removes it. Workloads load the alias in the model URI, `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion`. When the alias moves, a batch job picks up the new version at its next run without code changes, which decouples deployment from inference. A serving endpoint can be updated by looking up the alias version and calling the serving REST API. Several aliases can be set on one version in the UI, and the same alias name can point to only one version of a model at a time. Aliases replace the stages of the legacy registry.

concepts.heading: The Promotion Flow
concepts.body: A recommended flow has three stages, often run as jobs: train and register, then validate, then deploy. The validation task loads the model from Unity Catalog and runs checks such as format, metadata and performance on data slices. If checks pass the version receives the Challenger alias; otherwise the run stops and users can be notified, and a status tag records the outcome. The deployment task compares Challenger with Champion. Offline, both are scored on held-out data and results are tracked in MLflow; online, an A/B test or gradual rollout can split traffic on a serving endpoint. If Challenger is better, reassigning the Champion alias promotes it, and pointing the alias back at the earlier version rolls it back. With no existing Champion, compare to a business baseline. When retraining in production is too costly, `copy_model_version` copies a version from the staging model to the production model, and a Champion alias is set on the copy. Access control on the two registered models governs who can promote.

examPoints: A question about restricted production data, reviewed code and automated retraining is testing deploy code; a very expensive training run in one workspace without CI/CD is testing deploy models.
A question about labelling a version with a status such as validation_status, or removing that label, is testing model tags and the `set_model_version_tag` family, not aliases.
A question about a batch job or endpoint that must follow the production version without code edits is testing an alias such as Champion, loaded as `models:/name@Champion`.

quiz.q: A team retrains a demand model every week on production data. Code changes rarely, security forbids reading production data from the dev workspace, and every training script is peer reviewed. Which promotion strategy fits best?
choices: Train once in dev on a data sample and copy the artifact through staging to production, since training is a one-off job
Promote the model artifact only, because model files are the sole thing that differs between the environments
Train in production by hand once a quarter and skip staging tests, since the data cannot be reached from dev
Promote the code, so the pipeline trains in staging and production after review and tests
quiz.explain: Restricted production data and reviewed code are the stated reasons for deploy code: training runs in each environment and the production model is trained on production data. Deploy models would fail because dev cannot read the data.

quiz.q: A nightly batch scoring job must always use the production fraud model. Data scientists register new versions and promote them after validation, and the job code must not change on promotion. How should the job reference the model?
choices: Hard-code `models:/prod.ml_team.fraud/7` in the job and edit that version number each time a new version is promoted
Load `models:/prod.ml_team.fraud@Champion` and move the Champion alias to the new version when it is promoted
Add a tag `stage=production` to the promoted version and let the job read that tag at the start of every single run
Use the workspace registry Production stage so the job loads the newest version found in that stage on each run
quiz.explain: An alias is a mutable pointer, so the job resolves whichever version it names at run time. Version numbers need code edits, a tag only labels a version, and stages belong to the legacy registry.

days.recap: Prefer deploy code (train in every environment); deploy models fits costly training, one workspace and no CI/CD. Tags label models and versions (`set_model_version_tag`, needs APPLY TAG or ownership); aliases such as Champion and Challenger are movable pointers loaded as `models:/name@alias`. Validate, mark Challenger, compare, then reassign Champion.

days.title: Summary Statistics and Outlier Removal with Standard Deviation and IQR

concepts.heading: summary versus describe
concepts.body: Both methods return a new DataFrame of statistics for exploration. `df.describe()` gives count, mean, stddev, min and max for numeric and string columns, and you can pass column names such as `df.describe("age", "fare")`. `df.summary()` adds approximate quartiles, so with no arguments it returns count, mean, stddev, min, the 25%, 50% and 75% percentiles, and max. Unlike `describe`, `summary` accepts statistic names instead of columns: `df.summary("count", "min", "25%", "75%", "max")`, and any percentile can be written as a percentage string such as `"95%"`. To restrict columns, select first: `df.select("fare").summary("50%")`. The stddev is the sample standard deviation: the values 11, 12 and 13 give exactly 1.0. Both docs state they are meant for exploratory analysis and make no promise that the output schema stays stable, so use them to look at data, not as a pipeline contract. Percentiles in `summary` are approximate. When the question asks for a median or other percentile, `summary` is the answer; `describe` cannot give it.

concepts.heading: Reading the Output for Data Quality
concepts.body: The statistics are a first data-quality screen. The count of a column counts its non-null values, so a count below the table row count signals missing data; compare it with `df.count()`. Mean far from the median, or max far above the 75% percentile, suggests skew or outliers. A min of zero or a negative number in a column like age or price points to invalid codes. A stddev of zero means a constant column that carries no information for a model. For string columns only count, min and max are meaningful (min and max follow string ordering; mean and stddev make no sense for text), so they say nothing about category balance; use `groupBy().count()` for that. `dbutils.data.summarize(df)` also shows summary statistics with histograms in a notebook, but it is a Public Preview feature and analyzes the complete DataFrame, which can be very expensive for large data. For the exam and for stable practice, rely on `summary()` and `describe()`. On big data, compute them on the training split or a sample when exact full-data values are not required.

concepts.heading: Removing Outliers by Standard Deviation
concepts.body: The standard deviation rule keeps rows within k standard deviations of the mean, with k often 3. Compute the mean and `stddev` with an aggregation, collect the two numbers, then filter: keep rows where `abs(col - mean) <= k * sd`. For a column with mean 50 and standard deviation 10, k = 3 keeps values from 20 to 80, so 85 is removed. The rule fits roughly symmetric, bell-shaped data. Its weakness is that outliers inflate both the mean and the standard deviation, which widens the band and can hide the very points it should catch, and heavy skew makes the band cut one tail too much. Removal is a modeling decision: drop only values that are errors or irrelevant to the use case, because genuine extremes such as fraud may be exactly what the model must learn. Compute the limits on training data only and apply the same limits to new data, so validation rows do not shape the cutoffs. Filtering reduces the row count, so check how many rows were removed.

concepts.heading: Removing Outliers by IQR
concepts.body: The interquartile range rule uses quartiles, which a few extreme values hardly move. Get them with `df.approxQuantile("amount", [0.25, 0.75], 0.01)`; the last argument is the relative error, and zero would compute exact values at high cost. Null values are ignored in the calculation. Then IQR = Q3 - Q1, and the usual fences are Q1 - 1.5 * IQR and Q3 + 1.5 * IQR. With Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 50, IQR = 30, so the lower fence is -25 and the upper fence is 95; a row with 100 is an outlier, a row with 95 sits on the fence and is kept. Filter with `(col >= lower) & (col <= upper)`. Because the quartiles resist extremes and the rule makes no normality assumption, IQR is preferred for skewed data, and it is the convention behind box-plot whiskers. Increase the multiplier above 1.5 to remove fewer points. As with the standard deviation rule, derive the fences from training data and decide whether the outliers are errors before dropping them.

examPoints: A question that needs the median, a quartile or a chosen percentile in one call is testing `DataFrame.summary()` with percentage strings; describe gives only count, mean, stddev, min and max.

A question about data that is skewed or already contains extreme values is testing IQR fences from `approxQuantile`, while symmetric bell-shaped data fits the mean plus or minus k standard deviations rule.
A question about stable exam answers on summaries should use `summary()` or `describe()`; `dbutils.data.summarize` is Public Preview and analyzes the complete DataFrame.

quiz.q: An analyst needs the minimum, the median and the 95th percentile of the numeric column `fare` in a Spark DataFrame `df`, in a single call. Which code does it?
choices: `df.describe("fare")`, which reports the minimum and every percentile of that column
`df.select("fare").summary("min", "50%", "95%")`
`df.select("fare").describe("min", "50%", "95%")`, because describe takes statistic names for a single column
`df.agg(F.stddev("fare"))`, which returns the spread and the requested percentiles together
quiz.explain: summary accepts statistic names including percentages. describe takes column names and has no percentile output, so those arguments would be read as columns, and stddev is a single statistic.

quiz.q: For the column `amount`, `approxQuantile` returns Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 50, and the 1.5 x IQR rule is applied. The column holds the values -30, -25, 40, 95 and 100. Which values are removed?
choices: Only 100, because only values above the upper quartile can be outliers
-30, -25 and 100, because every value outside the quartiles is removed
100 and 95, because both are far above the median of the column
-30 and 100, because they fall outside the fences of -25 and 95
quiz.explain: IQR is 30, so the fences are 20 - 45 = -25 and 50 + 45 = 95. Values equal to a fence are kept, so -25 and 95 stay while -30 and 100 are removed.

days.recap: `describe()` gives count, mean, stddev, min, max; `summary()` adds approximate quartiles and accepts statistic names such as "95%". Standard deviation rule: keep within k sd of the mean (symmetric data). IQR rule: keep between Q1 - 1.5 IQR and Q3 + 1.5 IQR from `approxQuantile` (skewed data). Compute limits on training data and remove only real errors.

days.title: Visualizing Features and Comparing Two Features

concepts.heading: Charts for One Feature
concepts.body: Pick the chart from the feature type. For a continuous feature the first plot is a histogram, which splits the range into bins and shows how many rows fall in each, so you see skew, several clusters or a pile of zeros; the number of bins is configurable. A box chart summarizes the same feature through its quartiles, showing location, spread and skewness at a glance, with the outliers away from the box. For a categorical feature use a bar chart of counts per category, which reveals imbalance and rare levels that one-hot encoding will turn into sparse columns. A pie chart conveys proportions of a few categories, not time series, and it is hard to read with many slices. A counter display shows one number, and a word cloud suits text, so neither tells you about a distribution. Line charts fit ordered values such as time. These steps come before modeling decisions: a heavy right skew suggests a log transformation, and a rare category suggests grouping levels.

concepts.heading: Creating Visualizations in a Notebook
concepts.body: In a Databricks notebook, `display(df)` renders the result table. Click `+` above the result and choose Visualization to open the editor, pick a type such as histogram, bar, box, scatter or heatmap, and map columns to the axes, grouping and color. Histogram, bar, heatmap, scatter and pie charts use backend aggregation, so queries returning very large result sets are not truncated. Box charts are an exception: the documentation says they aggregate only up to a limited number of rows and truncate larger data, so aggregate or sample first. Cells can also show a data profile with summary statistics and visual insights for a DataFrame. For a custom plot with matplotlib or seaborn, bring a manageable sample to the driver, for example `df.sample(0.01).toPandas()`; never call `toPandas()` on a very large table. Visualizations can be added to a dashboard. The editor is a quick way to inspect features, whereas statistics are computed with `summary()` or aggregations.

concepts.heading: Comparing Two Continuous Features
concepts.body: To compare two continuous features use a scatter chart, which plots one against the other and can encode a third dimension, such as a category, by color. It shows direction, strength, curvature and outliers that a single number hides. Quantify the relationship with the Pearson correlation, `df.stat.corr("x", "y")` (also `df.corr`), which Spark currently supports with the pearson method only. It ranges from -1 to 1 and measures linear association; a perfect curve can still give a value near zero, so look at the scatter chart too. For many features at once, `pyspark.ml.stat.Correlation.corr(df, "features")` returns a correlation matrix over a vector column and supports pearson (default) and spearman, the rank-based method that captures monotonic relationships and is less affected by outliers; spearman is costly, so cache the input first. A correlation matrix can be displayed as a heatmap. Strongly correlated features carry redundant information, which matters for interpreting linear models.

concepts.heading: Comparing Categorical Features and Mixed Pairs
concepts.body: For two categorical features, build a contingency table of counts with `df.crosstab("plan", "churned")`: rows are the distinct values of the first column, columns the distinct values of the second, and absent pairs are zero. Show it as a grouped or stacked bar chart, or as a heatmap where color encodes the count or an aggregate. Compare proportions within each row to see whether the target rate changes by category. A scatter chart does not suit categories, and the Pearson correlation is meaningless for them. For a continuous feature split by a categorical one, such as income by region, use a box chart grouped by the category, or a bar chart of an aggregate such as the mean per group; the box chart also shows spread and outliers per group. For a continuous feature against a binary label, compare the distributions in each class. These comparisons guide which features to keep, whether to bin or encode them, and which interactions to explore.

examPoints: A question about the shape of one numeric column, skew or clusters, is testing a histogram or a box chart, while counts of one categorical column call for a bar chart.
A question about two numeric features is testing a scatter chart and Pearson correlation from `df.stat.corr`, which captures linear association only; spearman needs `pyspark.ml.stat.Correlation`.
A question about two categorical features is testing a `crosstab` contingency table shown as a grouped or stacked bar or heatmap; a numeric column split by a category is a grouped box chart.

quiz.q: A data scientist must compare how the continuous feature `income` is spread across four values of the categorical feature `region`, and spot outliers in each region. Which visualization answers this directly?
choices: A box chart of `income` grouped by `region`, which shows quartiles and outliers per region
A single pie chart of `income` split by `region`, which shows each region's share of the total income
A word cloud built from the `region` values, scaled by the frequency of each name in the table
A counter display of the average `income`, repeated in four cells for the four regions
quiz.explain: A grouped box chart shows median, spread and outliers for each category side by side. A pie shows only shares, a word cloud shows frequency, and a counter shows one average without distribution.

quiz.q: A practitioner suspects that the continuous features `tenure_months` and `monthly_spend` move together and wants both a picture and a single number for the strength of the linear relationship. What should be used?
choices: A bar chart of both columns and `df.crosstab("tenure_months", "monthly_spend")` for the strength
A histogram of `tenure_months` alone, which already contains the information about the other column
A scatter chart of the two columns and the Pearson correlation from `df.stat.corr`
A pie chart of `monthly_spend` bucketed by tenure, with the share as a measure of strength
quiz.explain: A scatter chart shows the joint pattern and Pearson correlation summarizes the linear strength. A crosstab suits categories, and a single-column histogram cannot show a relationship.

days.recap: One continuous feature: histogram or box chart; one categorical: bar chart of counts. Two continuous: scatter plus Pearson (`df.stat.corr`, linear only; spearman via `pyspark.ml.stat.Correlation`). Two categorical: `crosstab` shown as grouped bar or heatmap. Continuous by category: grouped box chart. Sample before `toPandas()`.

days.title: Imputing Missing Values and One-Hot Encoding Categorical Features

concepts.heading: Mean, Median or Mode
concepts.body: Imputation replaces missing values with a statistic of the observed ones. The mean uses all values and suits numeric features with a roughly symmetric distribution, but outliers drag it. The median is the middle value and resists extremes, so it is the safer choice for skewed numeric features such as income or prices. The mode is the most frequent value and is the only one of the three that works for categorical features; it also fits discrete codes. For the values 2, 3, 3, 4 and 100, the mean is 22.4, a value that none of the rows resembles, while the median and the mode are both 3. Imputation keeps rows that would otherwise be dropped, but it shrinks the variance of the feature and can hide the fact that a value was missing; if missingness itself is informative, add a separate flag column before filling. Compute the fill value from the training data only and reuse it for validation, test and new data, otherwise information leaks from the evaluation rows into training.

concepts.heading: Imputer in Spark ML
concepts.body: `pyspark.ml.feature.Imputer` completes missing values with the mean (default), median or mode of each column. Configure `strategy`, `inputCols` and `outputCols`, for example `Imputer(strategy="median", inputCols=["age", "income"], outputCols=["age_i", "income_i"])`. The input columns should be numeric; the docs warn that it does not support categorical features and may create incorrect values for them. It is an estimator: `fit(train_df)` computes the statistic of each column, ignoring missing entries, and returns an `ImputerModel` whose `transform` fills any DataFrame with those training values. All nulls count as missing, as does the configured `missingValue`, which defaults to NaN. The median comes from `approxQuantile` with a relative error of 0.001, so it is approximate. Placing the Imputer in a `Pipeline` guarantees that fit and transform use the same statistics. For a fixed constant, use `df.fillna(0, subset=["age"])` or a dictionary of column-to-value fills. These are plain replacements and do not learn anything from training data.

concepts.heading: Categorical Missing Values and the Mode
concepts.body: For a categorical column the Imputer is the wrong tool, so choose between two designs. One fills with the mode: find it with an aggregation (the `mode` function returns the most frequent value of a column) or with `groupBy(col).count()` sorted descending, then apply `df.fillna({"city": top_city})`. The other treats absence as information by filling with a label such as `"unknown"`, which keeps missingness visible and avoids inventing a real category. A string fill only affects string columns, because `fillna` ignores columns whose type does not match the value. If nulls are left in a string column, `StringIndexer` must decide: its `handleInvalid` option is `error` by default, `skip` drops the rows and `keep` assigns an extra index to unseen or null values. Do the filling before encoding. The mode is stable under outliers, but for a column with many categories of similar frequency it is a weak guess, so the unknown label is often preferable.

concepts.heading: One-Hot Encoding in Spark ML
concepts.body: Most models need numbers, and arbitrary integer codes would invent an order. One-hot encoding turns a category into a vector with a single 1. In Spark ML it takes two stages. `StringIndexer` maps strings to indices, by default ordered by frequency descending, so the most frequent label gets index 0. Then `OneHotEncoder` converts each index to a sparse binary vector. By default `dropLast=True`: the last category is dropped, because the entries would otherwise always sum to one and be linearly dependent. With 5 categories, index 2 becomes `[0, 0, 1, 0]` and index 4 becomes all zeros. With `handleInvalid="keep"` an extra category is added for invalid values, which is the all-zero vector when the last is dropped. Collect the encoded vectors and the numeric columns with `VectorAssembler`, then pass them to the estimator, all in a `Pipeline` fitted on training data so the same index mapping is applied to new rows. Encoding a column with thousands of levels creates very wide vectors.

examPoints: A question about a skewed numeric feature with extreme values and missing entries is testing median imputation; a categorical column with missing entries is testing mode (or an unknown label), not Imputer.
A question about fitting the fill values is testing that Imputer is an estimator: fit on the training data, transform every set, preferably inside a Pipeline.

A question about vector length after one-hot encoding is testing StringIndexer then OneHotEncoder with `dropLast` true: k categories produce vectors of length k - 1, and the dropped category is all zeros.

quiz.q: The numeric feature `household_income` is strongly right-skewed with a few very large values and 4 percent missing entries. Which imputation is most appropriate before training a linear regression?
choices: The mean of the observed values, because it uses every observation including the large ones
The mode of the observed values, because the most frequent value is always the best guess
Zero, because a missing income means that the household has no income at all
The median of the observed values, because it is not pulled toward the extreme incomes
quiz.explain: The median resists the large values that distort the mean in a skewed column. The mode suits categories and a constant of zero would invent a false value.

quiz.q: A `color` column has four values with these row counts: red 50, blue 30, green 15, gray 5. `StringIndexer` (default order) and `OneHotEncoder` (default `dropLast`) are applied. What does a gray row look like after encoding?
choices: An all-zero vector of length 3, because gray gets the last index, which is dropped
A vector of length 4 with a single 1 in the last position, because gray is the last color
A vector of length 3 with a 1 in the first position, because the rarest value is assigned index 0
An error, because the last category cannot be encoded when the last category is dropped by default
quiz.explain: Frequency-descending indexing gives red 0, blue 1, green 2 and gray 3. With the last category dropped, the vectors have length 3 and gray becomes all zeros.

days.recap: Mean for symmetric numeric data, median for skewed or outlier-heavy data, mode (or an unknown label) for categories. Imputer is an estimator for numeric columns: fit on training data, transform all sets. One-hot: StringIndexer (most frequent gets 0) then OneHotEncoder; default dropLast gives k - 1 entries, the last category is all zeros.

days.title: One-Hot Encoding Suitability and Log Transformations

concepts.heading: Nominal or Ordinal First
concepts.body: Before encoding, classify the column. A nominal feature such as colour, country or plan type has no order, so integer codes 0, 1, 2 would invent a ranking: a linear model would treat plan 2 as twice plan 1. One-hot encoding fixes this by creating one binary column per category, with a single 1 in each row. An ordinal feature such as shirt size S, M, L, XL has a real order, so an integer code 0, 1, 2, 3 keeps information that one-hot encoding throws away. If the steps between levels are very uneven, one-hot encoding still lets the model learn a separate effect per level. In Spark ML the usual route is `StringIndexer` (string to index, most frequent label gets 0 by default) followed by `OneHotEncoder`. `OneHotEncoder` drops the last category by default (`dropLast=True`), so a column with 4 categories becomes a vector of length 3 and the dropped category is the all-zeros vector. That avoids redundant columns that always sum to 1. Setting `handleInvalid` to `keep` maps unseen categories to an extra index instead of failing.

concepts.heading: Which Models Need One-Hot Encoding
concepts.body: The decision depends on the model family, not on the data alone. Models that treat numeric inputs as magnitudes or distances need a nominal feature expanded: linear and logistic regression, neural networks and k-nearest neighbours with Euclidean distance. The Spark guide says one-hot encoding lets algorithms that expect continuous features, such as logistic regression, use categorical features. Tree-based models (decision trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees) are different. When `StringIndexer` or `VectorIndexer` adds metadata to the DataFrame, Spark ML tree algorithms recognise the column as categorical and split on sets of categories, so the index is not read as a magnitude and `OneHotEncoder` is optional. A common practice is to compare both versions on a validation set. Because the tree sees the metadata, do not strip it by casting the indexed column to a plain number. One more case where one-hot encoding is not appropriate: an identifier-like column, such as a customer id, where one binary column per value would be as wide as the table is long.

concepts.heading: High-Cardinality Columns
concepts.body: A feature with tens of thousands of values, such as a merchant id or zip code, is a trap in two ways. One-hot encoding it produces a vector with one position per category, which strains memory and gives a linear model many weights to learn from few rows each. Spark ML trees have a separate limit: `maxBins` defaults to 32 and must be at least the number of categories of any categorical feature, so an index with 60,000 categories fails unless the cardinality is reduced or `maxBins` is raised, which makes training much slower. Remedies are generally accepted practice. Group rare levels into an `other` bucket, replace the id by aggregate features such as region, or use `FeatureHasher`, which hashes `column_name=value` into a vector of a dimension you choose. It behaves like one-hot encoding with a bounded width, and the price is that different values can collide in one position. `TargetEncoder` is another Estimator in the Spark guide; it replaces each category by an estimate from the label, so fit it on training data only, never on validation or test rows, whose labels would otherwise leak into the features.

concepts.heading: When a Log Transformation Is Appropriate
concepts.body: A log transform compresses large values much more than small ones: on a base-10 log, 1,000 becomes 3 and 1,000,000 becomes 6, so a thousand-fold gap shrinks to a difference of 3. It suits strictly positive features that span orders of magnitude or have a long right tail, such as income, lot area, response time or transaction amounts. Look at a histogram or the skewness first. A multiplicative relationship, where a percent change in the input gives a percent change in the output, becomes additive after the log, which matches the assumption of a linear model. A funnel-shaped residual plot (errors grow with the fitted value) is the usual sign that the target itself should be logged. It does not help bounded, symmetric or binary columns. Tree ensembles gain little because a split asks only whether a value is above a threshold and the log keeps the order of all values. The logarithm is undefined at zero and below; for counts with zeros use `log1p(x)`, which equals log(1 + x) and maps 0 to 0. Standardising changes scale, not shape, so it does not fix skew.

examPoints: A question that names a nominal string column and a linear, logistic, neural network or k-nearest-neighbours model is testing StringIndexer plus OneHotEncoder, while a random forest or boosted trees on an indexed column is testing that the index metadata makes one-hot encoding optional.

A question with a 60,000-value id column that fails in a Spark tree is testing maxBins (default 32) and the remedies: group rare levels, hash with FeatureHasher, or aggregate; an ordered feature such as shirt size is testing ordinal codes.
A question about a positive, right-skewed column, a funnel-shaped residual plot or zeros in a count column is testing the log transform, the log1p variant, and that tree models gain little from it.

quiz.q: A team trains a Spark ML `LogisticRegression` on a customer table. The column `plan_type` has 5 unordered string values, and a colleague passes its `StringIndexer` output directly into `VectorAssembler`. Training succeeds, but the coefficient for plan type is hard to interpret. What is the best change?
choices: Replace the indexer by a Bucketizer so that the plan values are grouped into numeric ranges the model can weigh
Keep the index, because a linear model reads the metadata and splits on categories exactly as a tree would
Add a OneHotEncoder after the indexer so each plan gets its own binary column, not an invented order
Cast the index to a string again, because logistic regression handles text columns when the label is binary
quiz.explain: The index 0 to 4 makes the model read plan 4 as four times plan 1, an order that does not exist. A one-hot vector gives each plan its own weight. Only tree algorithms use the indexer metadata, and a Bucketizer or string cast does not address the false ranking.

quiz.q: A data scientist logs a strictly positive, strongly right-skewed `revenue` column before training. Which statement about the effect is correct?
choices: A linear regression usually benefits, while a random forest changes little as splits use only value order
A random forest benefits most, because trees need symmetric inputs to find thresholds for their splits
Both models are unaffected, because the logarithm is a monotonic function that never changes a fitted model
Both models fail on this column, because the logarithm is only defined for values that are already between 0 and 1
quiz.explain: A log shrinks the tail and can make a multiplicative relationship additive, which helps a linear model. A tree only compares values with thresholds, and the log keeps their order, so the splits barely change. The log is defined for every positive number, not only between 0 and 1.

days.recap: Classify the column first: nominal needs one-hot (or hashing or grouping when it has very many values), ordinal can keep an order-preserving code. Linear models, neural networks and distance models need it; Spark ML trees read StringIndexer metadata, so one-hot is optional, and maxBins (default 32) limits categories. Log-transform positive, right-skewed columns for linear models, use log1p when zeros exist, and expect little change for trees.

days.title: Algorithm Selection, Class Imbalance, Estimators and Transformers, Pipelines

concepts.heading: Choosing an Algorithm from the Scenario
concepts.body: Start from the target. A continuous numeric label, such as minutes late, calls for regression (`LinearRegression`, `RandomForestRegressor`, `GBTRegressor`). A categorical label calls for classification (`LogisticRegression`, `RandomForestClassifier`, `GBTClassifier`). No label at all means unsupervised learning, for example `KMeans` for customer segments; k-means uses distances, so scale the features first, for instance with `StandardScaler`. Then read the other requirements in the stem. If regulators need one coefficient per feature, logistic or linear regression is the interpretable choice, because each coefficient states the direction and size of a feature's effect. For tabular data with non-linear effects, interactions and mixed numeric and categorical columns, tree ensembles are the usual fit: they need little scaling and find interactions on their own. Random forests average independent trees to reduce variance, while gradient-boosted trees build trees one after another to correct earlier errors. `PCA` is a feature transformer for dimensionality reduction and not a classifier.
