These are generally accepted guidelines, so match the algorithm to the label type first and to the constraint second.

concepts.heading: Mitigating Imbalanced Training Data
concepts.body: With 0.2% fraud rows, a model that always predicts not fraud scores 99.8% accuracy and is useless. Three families of remedies exist. Class weights give the rare class a larger weight in the loss, with no rows removed: Spark ML estimators such as `LogisticRegression` take a `weightCol`, and scikit-learn uses `class_weight="balanced"`. Undersampling keeps a fraction of the majority class: `train.sampleBy("label", {0: 0.1, 1: 1.0}, 42)` keeps about 10% of label 0 and every positive, at the cost of lost information. Oversampling repeats minority rows, and SMOTE from the single-node imbalanced-learn library instead creates synthetic rows by interpolating between neighbouring minority points. Two rules protect the evaluation. Split first and resample only the training part, because copies of one minority row on both sides of a split inflate the validation score. Evaluate on data with the natural class ratio, using recall, precision, F1 or area under the precision-recall curve, never accuracy alone.

concepts.heading: Estimators Versus Transformers
concepts.body: Spark ML defines two contracts. A `Transformer` has a `transform()` method that turns one DataFrame into another, usually by appending columns. `VectorAssembler` concatenates columns by a fixed rule and `Bucketizer` uses split points you provide, so neither learns from data and neither needs `fit()`. An `Estimator` has a `fit()` method that learns from a DataFrame and returns a `Model`, and that model is itself a Transformer. `LogisticRegression` is an Estimator: `fit()` returns a `LogisticRegressionModel` whose `transform()` appends `prediction`, `probability` and `rawPrediction`. `StandardScaler` is an Estimator too, because it must compute mean and standard deviation first and returns a `StandardScalerModel`. `StringIndexer` and `OneHotEncoder` are Estimators for the same reason, they must learn the categories. Calling `transform()` on an unfitted Estimator is therefore an error; call `fit()` first and then `transform()` on the returned model. The docs add that `fit()` and `transform()` are stateless, so an Estimator can be fit again on other data.

concepts.heading: Building a Training Pipeline
concepts.body: A `Pipeline` chains stages in order, for example `StringIndexer`, `OneHotEncoder`, `VectorAssembler`, `LogisticRegression`. A Pipeline is itself an Estimator. Its `fit()` calls `fit()` on every Estimator stage and `transform()` on every Transformer stage, passing the output DataFrame to the next stage, and returns a `PipelineModel`, which is a Transformer with the same number of stages in which every Estimator has become a fitted model. Saving and scoring with the `PipelineModel` guarantees that scoring data passes through the same fitted indexer, encoder and assembler, which is the reason to prefer it over saving only the final model. Stages must be listed in dependency order, because each stage reads columns written before it, and each stage must be a unique instance: reusing one `StandardScaler` object twice is not allowed, so create two instances. Parameters can be set on an instance (`lr.setMaxIter(10)`) or passed as a `ParamMap` to `fit()`, and a ParamMap overrides values set earlier. This is also what tuning tools rely on when they try parameter values.

examPoints: A question about a continuous label, a regulator-readable coefficient, mixed tabular features with interactions, or unlabeled customers is testing the match of label type and constraint to regression, logistic regression, tree ensembles or KMeans.

A question with a rare positive class is testing weightCol or class_weight, sampleBy undersampling, SMOTE as a single-node synthetic oversampler, and the rule to split first, resample only training and evaluate on the natural ratio.

A question about fit versus transform, what fit returns, or why a PipelineModel is saved is testing Estimator (fit returns a Model, a Transformer), Transformer (transform only), the Pipeline as an Estimator, and unique stage instances.

quiz.q: A data scientist calls `OneHotEncoder(inputCols=['idx'], outputCols=['vec']).transform(df)` and gets an error. The encoder has not been fit. What is the correct way to proceed, and what does the fit step return?
choices: Call `fit(df)` on the encoder, which returns a `OneHotEncoderModel` that can then transform the DataFrame
Call `transform` twice, because the first call learns the categories and the second call produces the vectors
Replace it by `VectorAssembler`, because only that stage can create the binary vector from an index column
Pass the encoder to `PipelineModel` directly, because a PipelineModel is the only object allowed to call transform
quiz.explain: The encoder must learn the number of categories, so it is an Estimator: `fit()` returns a model, which is a Transformer, and its `transform()` builds the vectors. Calling transform twice or using VectorAssembler does not learn anything, and a PipelineModel is produced by fitting a Pipeline.

quiz.q: A fraud table has 0.5% positive rows. A data scientist oversamples the positives by copying them, then randomly splits 80/20 and reports validation recall of 0.97, but production recall is far lower. Which change gives an honest estimate?
choices: Switch to accuracy on the validation set, because recall rises when rows are copied before the split
Split first, resample only the training part, and validate on data with the natural class ratio
Copy the positives a second time, so that the validation set contains more minority rows to measure recall
Remove all rows of the minority class from the validation set, so that no copy can appear on both sides
quiz.explain: Copies made before the split put identical minority rows in both training and validation, so the model is scored on rows it memorised. Resampling belongs only inside training, and the validation set keeps the production class ratio. More copies, accuracy or removing positives do not fix the leak.

days.recap: Pick the algorithm from the label type and the constraint (interpretable coefficients, tree ensembles for tabular interactions, KMeans for no label). For imbalance use class weights, sampleBy undersampling or SMOTE, split first, evaluate on the natural ratio with recall, precision or PR AUC. Estimators fit and return a Model (a Transformer); Transformers only transform; a Pipeline is an Estimator whose PipelineModel keeps training and scoring preprocessing identical.

days.title: Hyperparameter Tuning: Search Strategies, Optuna and Ray Tune, Parallelizing Single-Node Models

concepts.heading: Grid, Random and Bayesian Search
concepts.body: Grid search tries every combination of listed values, so its cost is the product of the value counts: 6 hyperparameters with 8 values each give 8^6 = 262,144 runs, while 3 x 4 x 2 = 24 is cheap enough for fast models. Grids are reproducible and give complete coverage of the listed values, which suits few hyperparameters. Random search draws each setting from a distribution and runs the number of trials you choose. It usually finds good values faster when only a few hyperparameters matter, because every trial tests a new value of each one: 60 random trials test 60 distinct values of the key hyperparameter, whereas a grid with 3 values per hyperparameter tests only 3. Bayesian optimization, such as TPE (the default Optuna sampler), also uses a chosen trial budget but builds a model of loss against hyperparameters and uses earlier results to pick the next setting, so it needs fewer trials to find a promising region. For scale-like parameters such as regularization strength or learning rate, sample on a log scale; in Optuna this is `trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 1e-1, log=True)`.

concepts.heading: Optuna and Ray Tune on Databricks
concepts.body: The Databricks tuning page lists three Python libraries: Optuna, Ray Tune and Hyperopt. Hyperopt is legacy: the open-source project is no longer maintained and is not included in Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning after 16.4 LTS ML, so `fmin`, `hp.*` and `SparkTrials` code needs a replacement, and Databricks recommends Optuna or Ray Tune. Optuna is light-weight and uses define-by-run search spaces: you write `objective(trial)` and ask the trial for values with `suggest_float`, `suggest_int` and `suggest_categorical`, so the space can depend on earlier choices. It is parallelized with Joblib and integrates with MLflow to track hyperparameters and metrics. With MLflow 3, `MlflowStorage` lets Optuna use the MLflow tracking server as shared storage, and `MlflowSparkStudy` runs parallel studies on PySpark executors through `optimize(objective, n_trials=8, n_jobs=4)`. Ray Tune comes with Ray, which Databricks Runtime ML includes, and uses Ray as its backend for distributed computing. Pick Ray Tune when the team already uses Ray, and Optuna for Spark executors or Joblib. Both avoid writing orchestration code.

concepts.heading: Parallelizing Single-Node Models
concepts.body: There are two ways to use a cluster for training. A distributed algorithm such as Spark MLlib already spreads one fit over all executors, so tune it with trials run one after another; starting many MLlib trials at once makes them compete for the same executors and gives no speed-up. A single-node model such as scikit-learn trains on one machine, so the cluster helps by running many independent trials at the same time, each trial one model fit on a worker. With 200 trials of a 4-minute fit, one machine needs 800 minutes, and 32 concurrent trials need roughly 7 rounds of 4 minutes, about 28 minutes. Concurrency is limited by the task slots on the workers. Two practical rules: workers cannot use the driver's SparkSession, so `spark.table(...)` inside the objective fails, and the data must be reachable as a storage path, a pandas array or a small broadcast sample. For thousands of small independent models, one per store, use `df.groupBy("store_id").applyInPandas(train_fn, schema)`, where each group is fit by a function.

concepts.heading: Parallelism Versus Adaptivity
concepts.body: Parallel trials speed up the search but have a cost for adaptive searchers. A Bayesian optimizer chooses each new setting from completed results. With 128 trials and 64 running at once, the first 64 suggestions are made with almost no history, so they are close to random, and only later rounds benefit. The legacy Databricks `SparkTrials` docs state the rule for fixed evaluation counts: greater parallelism speeds up the computation, while lower parallelism may lead to better results because each iteration has access to more past results. The same logic applies to any Bayesian tool, so raising concurrency from 4 to 64 can finish sooner while the best loss found is slightly worse. Random and grid search do not use earlier results, so they scale to full parallelism without that loss. Spark ML tuning has its own setting: `CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` evaluate parameter maps in serial by default, and `parallelism` of 2 or more evaluates several at once, within cluster resources. That shortens the wall-clock time but does not reduce the number of fits.

examPoints: A question with several hyperparameters and a trial budget is testing random or Bayesian search over a grid, while a small grid of fast models is testing exhaustive grid search; learning rate or regularization is tested through log-scale sampling.

A question about Ray, Joblib, Spark executors, MLflow tracking or an old Hyperopt SparkTrials notebook is testing Optuna (MlflowStorage, MlflowSparkStudy) and Ray Tune as the documented libraries, with Hyperopt as legacy.

A question contrasting scikit-learn and MLlib is testing parallel trials for single-node models versus sequential trials for distributed ones, applyInPandas for many small models, and the adaptivity loss at high concurrency.

quiz.q: A team tunes a Spark MLlib `RandomForestClassifier` on a very large DataFrame with Optuna. Each fit already uses every executor. How should the trials be scheduled?
choices: Run 64 trials at the same time so that the executors are shared between all of the model fits
Run the trials one after another so that each distributed fit can use the whole cluster
Convert the model to scikit-learn first, because distributed algorithms cannot be tuned at all
Use Hyperopt `SparkTrials` on the current runtime, because it is the only library for MLlib models
quiz.explain: Parallel trials of an already distributed trainer compete for the same executors and give no speed-up, so run them sequentially. Conversion is unnecessary because MLlib can be tuned, and Hyperopt is legacy and not in the runtime after 16.4 LTS ML.

quiz.q: A grid search for a model with 6 hyperparameters and 8 values each is planned, but the budget allows about 60 training runs. Which approach fits?
choices: Run the full grid, because it is the only method that is guaranteed to find the best value of every parameter
Cut the grid to 8 values for the first parameter and keep the others fixed at one value each
Use Bayesian optimization or random search with 60 trials, sampling scale-like parameters on a log scale
Use `CrossValidator` with 60 folds, because the number of folds sets the number of trials of the search
quiz.explain: The full grid has 8^6 = 262,144 runs. Random search or Bayesian optimization takes a trial budget you choose, and log sampling covers each order of magnitude. Tuning one parameter ignores the rest, and the number of folds is not the number of trials.

days.recap: Grid cost is the product of value counts (8^6 = 262,144); random and Bayesian search take a chosen budget, Bayesian uses earlier results, and log scales suit learning rates and regularization. Teach Optuna (define-by-run, MLflow, MlflowSparkStudy) and Ray Tune; Hyperopt is legacy and absent after 16.4 LTS ML. Single-node models tune with parallel trials, distributed MLlib sequentially; high concurrency weakens adaptive search.

days.title: Cross-Validation Versus Train-Validation Split, Performing It and Counting Models

concepts.heading: Two Validation Methods Compared
concepts.body: A train-validation split creates one (training, validation) pair, for example `trainRatio=0.8`, and evaluates each parameter combination once. In Spark ML this is `TrainValidationSplit`. Its cost is one fit per setting, but the estimate depends on one random split, so it is less reliable when the data is small. K-fold cross-validation, `CrossValidator` in Spark ML, splits the data into k folds, trains k times with each fold held out once, and averages the metric. Every row is used for both training and validation across the folds, the average has a lower variance than a single split, and the price is k times the training cost. The Spark docs say `TrainValidationSplit` is less expensive but will not produce results as reliable when the training dataset is not large. So pick the split for very large data or a tight compute budget, because millions of validation rows are already a stable estimate, and pick cross-validation for small or medium data. Both finally refit the estimator with the best parameters on the entire dataset passed to `fit`.

concepts.heading: Performing Cross-Validation in Spark ML and scikit-learn
concepts.body: `CrossValidator` needs three things: an `Estimator` (an algorithm or a whole `Pipeline`), a list of `ParamMap`s usually built with `ParamGridBuilder().addGrid(lr.regParam, [0.01, 0.1]).build()`, and an `Evaluator` such as `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` or `RegressionEvaluator` that supplies the metric. `numFolds` sets k, and the evaluator's `metricName` overrides its default metric. Passing a Pipeline as the estimator refits the scaler, indexer or imputer on the training folds of each split, which avoids leaking validation statistics into preprocessing. `fit(train_df)` returns a `CrossValidatorModel`: `bestModel` is the refit on all training data, and `avgMetrics` holds one averaged metric per ParamMap, in grid order. Setting `parallelism` to 2 or more evaluates parameter maps concurrently. Keep the test DataFrame out of `fit` and score it once afterwards. In scikit-learn, `cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="f1")` returns an array of 5 scores, one per fold, which you usually summarize with `scores.mean()`. It searches nothing and returns no fitted model. For rare classes use stratified folds, and for time series validate on later periods instead of random folds.

concepts.heading: Counting the Models Trained
concepts.body: The grid is the Cartesian product of the value lists, so 3 values of `regParam` and 4 values of `maxIter` give 3 x 4 = 12 parameter maps. With `CrossValidator(numFolds=5)` the search runs combinations x folds = 12 x 5 = 60 fits, and the final refit on the entire dataset adds one more, 61 in total. The exam may ask for either number, so read whether the question says including or not counting the final model. With `TrainValidationSplit` each combination is fit once: a 3 x 2 grid gives 6 fits in the search and 7 with the final model. Changing both factors multiplies the cost. A grid of 4 x 3 = 12 combinations with 3 folds is 36 fits; adding two values to the second hyperparameter and moving to 5 folds gives 4 x 5 = 20 combinations x 5 = 100 fits, about 2.8 times as many. Switching a 4 x 4 x 4 grid from 5 folds (64 x 5 = 320 fits) to a single split gives 64 fits. `parallelism` shortens the wall-clock time but not the count.

concepts.heading: Leakage and Validation Design
concepts.body: A validation score is only as honest as the split. If a scaler is fit on all rows before `CrossValidator` runs, the means and standard deviations of the validation folds have already shaped the training data; with imputers, target encoders, feature selection or PCA the leak can be large. The fix is to pass the Pipeline to the tuner. Random k-fold also assumes independent rows. For two years of daily sales, a random fold trains on April rows to predict March, so the offline score is inflated; use a time-ordered split with a date cutoff or `TimeSeriesSplit`, training on the past and validating on a later period. For a 0.5% positive label, a random fold can hold no positives, so use stratified folds that keep the class ratio in every fold (scikit-learn `StratifiedKFold`; Spark's `CrossValidator` has no stratified option, only a `foldCol` for your own folds), while remembering that stratification does not add positive rows. Keep a test set outside tuning. Cross-validation estimates how the choice generalizes to similar data, and the held-out test gives the final unbiased check of the chosen model.

examPoints: A question on 600 million rows and a limited budget is testing TrainValidationSplit (one fit per setting), while 900 rows with a one-point accuracy difference is testing CrossValidator (average of k folds, k times the cost).

A question listing CrossValidator inputs is testing Estimator or Pipeline, ParamGridBuilder maps and an Evaluator, with bestModel refit on the entire dataset, avgMetrics per ParamMap, and parallelism affecting time only.

A question asking how many models are trained is testing combinations x folds (3 x 4 x 5 = 60, plus 1 for the final refit) or combinations x 1 for TrainValidationSplit; read whether the final model is counted.

quiz.q: A data scientist builds a grid with 3 values of `numTrees` and 5 values of `maxDepth` and tunes a Spark ML `RandomForestRegressor` with `CrossValidator(numFolds=4)`. How many models are trained in total, including the final model fitted with the best parameters on the whole training data?
choices: 16, because each of the four folds trains one model with the best parameters
61, because the grid has 15 combinations and each is fitted in four folds
15, because the search fits each combination once and then keeps the best
60, because the final refit on the whole data is not a trained model
quiz.explain: The grid has 3 x 5 = 15 combinations, each fitted in 4 folds: 60 fits in the search. The final refit with the best parameters on the entire dataset is one more fit, so 61. Counting 60 leaves out the refit, and 15 is the number of fits of a TrainValidationSplit search.

quiz.q: A forecasting team compares models on two years of daily sales with random 5-fold cross-validation. Offline error is low, but production error is much higher. What is the most likely reason and fix?
choices: The grid is too large, so the team should lower `parallelism` to evaluate fewer parameter maps at once
Five folds are too few, so the team should use 50 folds and keep the random assignment of days
The metric is wrong, so the team should switch from RMSE to R-squared and keep the same folds
Random folds train on future days, so validate on later periods with a time-ordered split
quiz.explain: With correlated daily data, random folds put later days into the training data for earlier validation days, which inflates the score. A time-ordered split trains on the past and validates on a later period. More folds, another metric or a different parallelism value keep the leakage.

days.recap: Use TrainValidationSplit for big data and tight budgets (one fit per setting), CrossValidator for small or medium data (k fits, averaged). CrossValidator takes an Estimator or Pipeline, ParamMaps and an Evaluator, refits bestModel on all data, and parallelism changes time, not counts. Models = combinations x folds (3 x 4 x 5 = 60, 61 with the refit). Avoid leakage with pipelines, time-ordered splits and stratified folds.

days.title: Classification and Regression Metrics and Choosing a Metric

concepts.heading: Classification Metrics from the Confusion Matrix
concepts.body: Take 1,000 rows with 100 positives. The model flags 50 rows: 40 true positives (TP) and 10 false positives (FP), so 60 positives are missed (FN) and 890 negatives are correctly cleared (TN). Accuracy = (40 + 890) / 1000 = 0.93, although it misses most positives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.80. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 100 = 0.40. F1 is the harmonic mean, 2 x 0.80 x 0.40 / 1.20 = 0.533; the harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so poor recall cannot hide behind high precision. With precision 0.90 and recall 0.30 the F1 is 0.45. Accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced, because always predicting the majority class gives 99.7% accuracy with 0.3% positives. These are generally accepted definitions. In Spark ML, `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator` offers `f1` (its default, a weighted average over classes), `accuracy`, `precisionByLabel`, `recallByLabel`, `fMeasureByLabel` and `logLoss`; `metricLabel` selects the class for the by-label metrics.

concepts.heading: Log Loss, ROC AUC and PR AUC
concepts.body: These three work on scores instead of hard labels. Log loss averages the negative log of the probability the model gave to the true class, so it punishes confident wrong answers heavily and lower is better. Two models with the same 90% accuracy differ: one whose errors sit near probability 0.5 has a lower log loss than one whose errors sit near 0.99 for the wrong class. Spark computes it with `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(metricName="logLoss")`, which reads the `probability` column. ROC AUC is the area under the curve of true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds, and measures how well scores rank positives above negatives; 0.5 means ranking by chance. PR AUC is the area under precision against recall and focuses on the positive class, so it is more informative when positives are rare, while ROC AUC can look high because many negatives keep the false positive rate small. `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` supports `areaUnderROC` (default) and `areaUnderPR`, using a `rawPrediction` column. If you feed it hard 0/1 predictions the ROC has one point, and with TPR 0.80 and TNR 0.90 the area is (1 + 0.80 - 0.10) / 2 = 0.85.

concepts.heading: Regression Metrics
concepts.body: `RegressionEvaluator` supports `rmse` (the default), `mse`, `r2`, `mae` and `var`. Take errors of 2, 2, 2 and 10 minutes. MAE is the mean absolute error: (2 + 2 + 2 + 10) / 4 = 4. RMSE squares first: sqrt((4 + 4 + 4 + 100) / 4) = sqrt(28) = about 5.29. RMSE is never smaller than MAE, and the gap grows when a few errors are large, because squaring lets them dominate. Both are in the label's units, unlike MSE, which is in squared units. R-squared = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot compares the model with predicting the mean label. For labels 2, 4, 6, 8 (mean 5, SS_tot = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20) and predictions 3, 3, 7, 7 (SS_res = 4), r2 = 1 - 4 / 20 = 0.8. A value of 0 means no better than the mean and a negative value means worse than the mean, which is possible on held-out data. Smaller is better for rmse, mse and mae, larger is better for r2; the evaluator's `isLargerBetter` tells the tuner which direction to optimize.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Metric for the Objective
concepts.body: Match the metric to the cost of each error type. If a missed positive is the costly error, as in screening patients for a follow-up test, prioritize recall (TP / (TP + FN)), usually by lowering the threshold and accepting lower precision. If a false alarm is the costly error, as in a spam filter that hides legitimate mail, prioritize precision. For one threshold-free comparison with rare fraud, use areaUnderPR, and avoid accuracy and hammingLoss, which the majority class dominates. F1 balances precision and recall when both matter. Use log loss when the probabilities themselves are used, for example for risk scores or expected-cost decisions. For regression, use mae when a few extreme records are noise and every minute of error should count the same, rmse when large misses are especially costly, and r2 for the share of label variance explained, which has no unit. When tuning with `CrossValidator`, set the same metric on the evaluator, because it ranks the parameter maps by that metric and by nothing else.

examPoints: A question giving TP, FP, FN and TN or a precision and recall is testing accuracy, precision, recall and F1 as the harmonic mean (0.90 and 0.30 give 0.45), and that accuracy misleads under imbalance.

A question about probabilities or ranking is testing logLoss (MulticlassClassificationEvaluator, probability column), areaUnderROC as the default and areaUnderPR for rare positives in BinaryClassificationEvaluator.

A question on delivery times or outliers is testing rmse (default, in label units, penalizes large errors) versus mae (linear) and r2 (relative to the mean, negative if worse), and a costly miss or false alarm is testing recall versus precision.

quiz.q: A model is evaluated on 1,000 rows with 100 positives. It flags 50 rows, of which 40 are truly positive. Which pair of values is correct for the positive class?
choices: Precision 0.40 and recall 0.80, since precision divides the true positives by the actual positives
Precision 0.80 and recall 0.93, since recall counts all of the correct predictions in the data
Precision 0.93 and recall 0.40, since precision counts the negatives that were cleared correctly
Precision 0.80 and recall 0.40, since recall divides the true positives by the actual positives
quiz.explain: Precision = 40 / 50 = 0.80 (flagged rows that are positive) and recall = 40 / 100 = 0.40 (actual positives found). The accuracy of 0.93 comes from the 890 correctly cleared negatives. The other pairs swap the definitions or use accuracy.

quiz.q: A delivery-time model makes absolute errors of 2, 2, 2 and 10 minutes, and a few records are known to have wrong timestamps. The team wants a metric in minutes that does not let extreme records dominate. Which metric and value fit?
choices: `mae`, which equals 4 minutes because each error counts linearly
`rmse`, which equals 4 minutes because it averages the errors without any squaring
`rmse`, which equals about 5.29 minutes because the squaring reduces the weight of large errors
`r2`, which equals 4 minutes because it reports the average error in the unit of the label
quiz.explain: MAE = (2 + 2 + 2 + 10) / 4 = 4 minutes, with a linear penalty. RMSE = sqrt(28) = about 5.29 and gives the 10-minute miss more weight, not less. R-squared has no unit and compares the model with the mean label.

days.recap: Classification: precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = harmonic mean (0.90 and 0.30 give 0.45); accuracy misleads under imbalance. logLoss needs probabilities, areaUnderROC is the default and areaUnderPR suits rare positives. Regression: rmse (default) penalizes large errors, mae is linear, r2 compares with the mean and can be negative. Choose recall when misses cost most, precision when false alarms do.

days.title: Log Targets, Exponentiation, Bias-Variance and Model Complexity

concepts.heading: Why a log target must be exponentiated
concepts.body: When a model is trained on ln(revenue), every prediction it returns is also a logarithm, and so is every error computed from it. To report revenue, apply the inverse transform exp to the predictions and compare them with the original, unlogged label. If the target was log1p(y), the inverse is expm1. Example with three stores whose true revenue is 250, 1000 and 4000: the model predicts 5.7, 6.8 and 8.5 on the log scale. The true logs are 5.52, 6.91 and 8.29, so the RMSE on the log scale is about 0.17. After exp the predictions are about 299, 898 and 4915, the errors are about 49, minus 102 and 915, and the RMSE in currency is about 532. The two figures cannot be compared with each other. One more caution: exp of a mean of logs is the geometric mean, a median-type value, so exp(prediction) estimates the typical revenue and tends to sit below the mean; with normal log errors of standard deviation 0.5 the mean is about 13 percent higher.

concepts.heading: When no inverse transform is needed
concepts.body: Exponentiation is required only when a number must mean something in the original unit: a forecast shown to finance, an RMSE or MAE in currency, or a comparison with a model trained on the raw label. Several tasks stay on the log scale without any inverse. Ranking two candidates that both predict ln(y) by their RMSE on one shared validation set is consistent, because both are measured the same way. Residual plots against fitted values are normally drawn on the scale the model was fitted on, and the log scale is often what makes the spread even. Feature importance also describes the fitted model, not the unit. Interpretation has its own rule: in a linear model with a log target, a coefficient of 0.05 multiplies the prediction by exp(0.05), about 1.051, so a one-unit rise in that feature raises the predicted value by roughly 5.1 percent. Never compare an RMSE on the log scale with an RMSE on the raw scale.

concepts.heading: Bias, variance and the reading of two errors
concepts.body: Prediction error splits into bias, variance and irreducible noise. Bias is systematic error from a model too simple for the signal. Variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample. Noise cannot be removed by any model. The diagnosis comes from comparing training and validation error. If both are high and close, for example a straight line fitted to a curved relationship with RMSE 11.9 and 12.3, the model underfits: high bias. Fix it with more expressive features such as polynomial terms, a more flexible model, or weaker regularization. If training error is very low and validation error is much higher, for example RMSE 2.1 against 14.8 for a very deep forest, the model memorizes noise: high variance, or overfitting. Fix it with a simpler model, stronger regularization, fewer features or more training data. Collecting more rows does not cure underfitting.

concepts.heading: Choosing complexity with a validation curve
concepts.body: Complexity is the dial between the two failures. Training error keeps falling as complexity grows, so it can never choose the model. Validation error falls while bias shrinks and then rises as variance takes over, forming a U. Pick the complexity at the bottom of that curve. Suppose polynomial degrees 1 to 6 give training RMSE 8.0, 5.5, 3.9, 2.6, 1.4 and 0.5 and validation RMSE 8.4, 5.9, 4.4, 4.1, 5.2 and 7.8. The gaps are 0.4, 0.4, 0.5, 1.5, 3.8 and 7.3. Degree 4 has the lowest validation RMSE, 4.1, so it is the choice; degrees 1 to 3 underfit and degrees 5 and 6 overfit. For tree models in Spark ML the complexity knobs are maxDepth, where lower means simpler, and minInstancesPerNode, where higher means simpler. Let CrossValidator or TrainValidationSplit with an evaluator read the validation score instead of tuning by hand.

examPoints: A question that asks for revenue in dollars, or an RMSE in the original unit, from a model trained on a logged label is testing exp (or expm1 for log1p) before the metric; ranking candidates on one shared split on the log scale needs no inverse.

A question with a low training error and a much higher validation error is testing high variance: reduce depth, raise minInstancesPerNode, regularize or add data; two high, close errors point to high bias and call for a more flexible model.
A question that lists validation error for several complexities is testing the U-shaped curve: choose the lowest validation error, never the lowest training error.

quiz.q: A gradient-boosted model is trained on ln(price). For one house with a true price of 250 (ln 250 is about 5.52) it predicts 5.7. The business wants the error in currency units. What is correct?
choices: Report 250 minus 5.7 as the error, since the logged label was only used during training
Divide the prediction 5.7 by ln(250) to rescale it and report a ratio close to 1.03
Apply exp to 5.7, about 299, and compare it with 250 for an error near 49
Add 5.7 to 250 and divide by two, which averages the two scales into currency units
quiz.explain: The model's outputs are logarithms, so exp turns 5.7 back into about 299 currency units, which is then compared with the true 250. Subtracting a logarithm from a price, dividing by a logarithm or averaging the two scales mixes units and gives no valid error.

quiz.q: Regression trees of maxDepth 2, 4, 8 and 16 give training RMSE 9.0, 6.5, 3.1 and 0.9 and validation RMSE 9.4, 7.0, 7.6 and 10.2. Which statement is right?
choices: Depth 4 has the lowest validation RMSE, and depth 16 shows high variance from its gap
Depth 16 is best because its training RMSE is the lowest and its model captures the most signal available
Depth 2 is best because the simplest model always generalizes better than any deeper tree
Depth 8 is best because it sits halfway between the training and validation errors of its neighbors
quiz.explain: Validation RMSE bottoms out at 7.0 for depth 4, so that is the choice, while depth 16 has a training RMSE of 0.9 against 10.2 on validation, a gap of 9.3 that signals overfitting. Training error alone cannot choose a model, and simplicity is not always best, because depth 2 underfits with 9.4.

days.recap: A log target gives log predictions: apply exp (expm1 for log1p) before reporting in the original unit or computing a currency error, and compare candidates on one shared scale. Diagnose with the gap: low training and high validation error is variance, two high close errors are bias. Choose the complexity at the minimum of the validation curve, using maxDepth, minInstancesPerNode and cross-validation.

days.title: Serving Modes, Custom Model Endpoints and Batch Inference with pandas and Spark

concepts.heading: Batch, real-time and streaming: choose by how the result is consumed
concepts.body: Three deployment modes answer one question: when does the input exist and who waits for the answer? Batch inference runs a model over a bounded set of rows on a schedule and stores the predictions, usually in a Delta table. Consumers read them later, so per-row latency is irrelevant and throughput and cost matter. Real-time inference keeps the model behind a REST endpoint on Mosaic AI Model Serving, which runs on serverless compute and scales with demand: a caller sends input and waits for the prediction. Streaming inference scores events continuously as they arrive and writes the results to a table, with freshness of seconds to minutes and nobody waiting. A nightly churn score for 40 million customers is batch. A fraud score returned while the customer is at checkout is real-time, because the input exists only in that request. The price of batch is staleness: a new row has no score until the next run.

concepts.heading: Deploying a custom model to an endpoint
concepts.body: Databricks calls traditional ML or Python models packaged in MLflow format custom models, for example scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch and Hugging Face transformer models. The path to an endpoint has three steps: log the model with MLflow, register it in Unity Catalog, then create a serving endpoint whose served entity is that model version. A signature, which records input and output schema, is recommended and is required to register a model in Unity Catalog. Arbitrary Python, such as cleaning requests before calling an estimator, is wrapped in a custom mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel with a predict method, so the preprocessing is served with the model and cannot drift from training. Size the endpoint by concurrency, roughly queries per second times model execution time: 20 requests per second at 0.15 seconds each need about 3 concurrent requests. Scale to zero saves cost on rarely used endpoints but adds a cold start and is not recommended for production. The creator identity of an endpoint is fixed, so create production endpoints under a long-lived service principal.

concepts.heading: Batch inference with pandas and with a Spark UDF
concepts.body: Pick the scoring pattern by data size. When the rows fit in memory on one node, load the registered model and score a pandas DataFrame: model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(model_uri) followed by preds = model.predict(pdf). It works for any flavor and needs no Spark. When the table is large, such as 600 million rows, calling toPandas would pull everything onto the driver. Instead export the model as a Spark UDF with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, model_uri) and add the column with df.withColumn('prediction', udf()), so scoring runs in parallel on the executors and the result is written back to Delta. Calling the UDF without arguments uses the columns named in the model signature. Both patterns exist only for scoring: a pyfunc model has predict, not fit, and a Spark DataFrame has no predict method. Retraining on the scoring data or calling an endpoint once per row are not batch inference.

concepts.heading: Loading by alias and restoring dependencies
concepts.body: A Unity Catalog alias is a mutable name for one model version, such as Champion. The URI models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion resolves to whichever version the alias points to at run time. The Databricks lifecycle page uses exactly this for batch inference: when the Champion alias is moved to a new version, the next run of the workload picks it up, so deploying a model is decoupled from the job. The job needs EXECUTE on the model plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG. Pinning a version number in code forces an edit and redeploy after every promotion, and a copy of the files in a volume goes stale. If the cluster has different library versions from the ones the model was logged with, pass env_manager='virtualenv' to spark_udf. This restores the model's dependencies in the context of the UDF only and leaves the notebook's own libraries untouched. For a pyfunc model in a notebook, mlflow.pyfunc.get_model_dependencies returns a requirements file to install.

examPoints: A question that describes a stored result read later, or an input set known in advance, is testing batch inference; per-request input that a caller waits on is testing a real-time Model Serving endpoint; an unbounded event feed scored in seconds to minutes with no one waiting is streaming.

A question on getting a scikit-learn or custom model online is testing the order log with MLflow (signature included), register in Unity Catalog, create the endpoint, with a custom pyfunc when preprocessing must travel with the model.

A question on scoring a registered model is testing size: pandas load_model and predict when the data fits on one node, spark_udf with withColumn when it does not, and an alias URI when the job must follow the Champion version.

quiz.q: A bank wants the mobile app to show a loan offer within a second after a customer types income and amount into a form. The inputs exist only when the customer submits. Which deployment fits?
choices: A nightly job scores every customer and writes offers to a Delta table that the app reads
A weekly job that retrains the model and precomputes offers for all known customers in advance
A streaming pipeline in triggered mode that rescores the whole customer history each hour
A model serving endpoint that the app calls with the form values and gets the offer back
quiz.explain: The inputs exist only at request time and a person waits, so an online endpoint is required. A precomputed table has no row for values that were just typed, and hourly or nightly refreshes cannot meet a one second target.

quiz.q: A registered model must score a 70-million-row Delta table every night. The job must follow whichever version holds the Champion alias without code edits, and the output goes to another table. What should the job do?
choices: Call toPandas on the table, load the newest version number from a note in the job and score on the driver
Load the alias URI in spark_udf, add the prediction with withColumn and write the result to Delta
Create an endpoint and send one REST request per row from a loop, using the version listed in the code
Copy the model files to a volume once, and have each night's run read that copy and score row by row
quiz.explain: The alias URI resolves to the current Champion version on each run, and spark_udf scores in parallel on the executors so the table never has to fit on the driver. toPandas, a request per row and a fixed copy of the files fail on scale or keep an outdated version.

days.recap: Choose the mode by consumption: stored results read later are batch, a caller waiting is a real-time endpoint, an endless feed with no waiting is streaming. A custom model is logged with MLflow, registered in Unity Catalog and served from an endpoint, with pyfunc for extra code. Score with pandas load_model and predict on one node, with spark_udf and withColumn at scale, and load by alias so promotion needs no job edit.

days.title: Streaming Inference, Real-Time Endpoints and Traffic Splitting

concepts.heading: Streaming inference with pipelines and Structured Streaming
concepts.body: Streaming inference scores events as they arrive and appends the results to a table. There is no separate inference page for pipelines, so the pattern is Structured Streaming plus the Spark UDF from mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf, which the Databricks docs describe as scoring on a cluster either as a batch job or as a Spark Streaming job. In Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines, formerly Delta Live Tables, a streaming table suits append-only events: each record is processed once and a row already appended is not re-read. A checkpoint lets a restarted query resume without rescoring. This has a consequence for models: if the query is changed from model version 1 to version 2 and a normal update runs, old rows keep their version 1 scores and only new rows get version 2, until a full refresh requeries all the source data. Triggered mode refreshes available data and stops, which fits freshness of every 10 minutes or longer. Continuous mode keeps tables fresh as data arrives, which fits 10 seconds to a few minutes.

concepts.heading: Bounded state and the right dataset type
concepts.body: Streaming tables are built for low-latency streaming over bounded state. They expect streams that are naturally bounded, with a defined start and end such as a finite set of files, or bounded by a watermark. A watermark tells Structured Streaming how long to wait for late events before a time window is complete, so old state can be dropped. A windowed feature computed on a stream with no end and no watermark can make the pipeline fail from memory pressure. Raising partitions, switching to a view or running a full refresh at every update does not bound the state. Choose the dataset by the source: a streaming table for append-only sources scored once, a materialized view when results must be recomputed as data changes, for example a join whose dimension rows are updated, because a streaming table does not recompute joins when dimensions change. A view is evaluated on demand and not persisted, so it suits intermediate steps.

concepts.heading: Querying a real-time endpoint
concepts.body: A deployed endpoint answers REST calls at https://<instance>/serving-endpoints/<name>/invocations. For custom models the body is JSON in one of two pandas formats. The recommended dataframe_split carries index, columns and data, so column order is explicit. dataframe_records sends one JSON object per row and does not guarantee column ordering, which can make a model read the wrong column. Tensor models accept the TensorFlow Serving formats, for example the columnar {'inputs': [[5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2]]}. The response wraps the output in a predictions key. For authentication, Databricks recommends machine-to-machine OAuth tokens in production, and for testing a personal access token belonging to a service principal rather than to a user. Route optimization, which can only be enabled when the endpoint is created, lowers overhead latency and raises throughput for high-QPS endpoints, but a route-optimized endpoint accepts only OAuth tokens, not personal access tokens, and must be queried at its own dedicated URL, so existing clients that used the usual URL and a token stop working.

concepts.heading: Splitting traffic between served models
concepts.body: One endpoint can host several served entities, for instance the current model and a challenger. The endpoint config lists the served entities and a traffic_config whose routes assign each a traffic_percentage. The docs example gives current 90 and challenger 10, so 9 of every 10 requests go to the current version while clients keep one endpoint URL. This supports A/B tests and gradual rollout. To test the challenger alone, post to /serving-endpoints/<endpoint>/served-models/<served-model-name>/invocations, which ignores the traffic settings. All served entities on one endpoint must be the same model type: a custom model and an external model cannot share an endpoint, so compare those with two endpoints. The split is changed with the endpoint config update API or Edit configuration in the Serving UI. Until the new configuration is ready, the old one keeps serving, and only one update can run at a time.

examPoints: A question that scores a stream and must survive restarts is testing Structured Streaming with spark_udf, a streaming table and a checkpoint; a question where old rows still show model version 1 after a swap is testing that only a full refresh recomputes them.

A question on querying an endpoint is testing dataframe_split (recommended, ordered columns), the predictions key, OAuth M2M tokens for production, and the OAuth-only dedicated URL of a route-optimized endpoint.

A question that sends 90 percent to the current model and 10 percent to a challenger on one name is testing traffic_config and traffic_percentage; the served-models path bypasses the split, and custom and external models cannot be mixed.

quiz.q: A pipeline's streaming table adds a score column with model version 1. The team edits the query to use version 2 and runs a normal update. They want every stored row to carry a version 2 score. What should they do?
choices: Nothing, since each normal update rescores all stored rows with the latest query text
Run a full refresh, which requeries the source data so earlier rows are scored with version 2
Switch the pipeline from triggered to continuous mode, which rewrites the scores already stored
Delete the checkpoint of a different query and rely on the watermark to recompute old rows
quiz.explain: A streaming table reads each record once, so after a normal update old rows keep version 1 scores and only new rows get version 2. A full refresh requeries all earlier data. Pipeline mode only controls when updates run, and a watermark limits state, not past scores.

quiz.q: An endpoint serves current at 75 percent and challenger at 25 percent. An engineer must run a smoke test that reaches only the challenger without changing the split. Which approach works?
choices: Delete the current served entity until the test has finished, then add it back again afterwards
Add the field traffic_percentage with a value of 100 to the body that is sent to the normal URL
Send the request with a header X-Served-Model set to challenger to the normal endpoint URL address
Post to the served-models path of challenger, which ignores traffic settings
quiz.explain: Each served entity has its own invocations path under served-models, and querying it ignores the traffic settings, so production routing is untouched. Deleting the current entity disrupts production, and neither a body field nor a custom header selects a served model.

days.recap: Streaming inference is Structured Streaming plus spark_udf; a streaming table scores each record once, so a model swap affects only new rows until a full refresh, and unbounded state needs a watermark. Query endpoints with dataframe_split, expect a predictions key, use M2M OAuth in production, and note that route optimization means OAuth and a dedicated URL. Split traffic with traffic_percentage per served entity on one endpoint of one model type, and test one entity through its served-models path.

days.title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Four Domains

concepts.heading: Domain 1, Databricks Machine Learning (38 percent, the heaviest)
concepts.body: This domain has 18 tasks and 38 percent of the 48 scored questions, so it carries the most points. MLOps: Databricks recommends the deploy code pattern, where training code moves from development to staging to production and the model is trained in each environment, over promoting a finished artifact. ML Runtime bundles tested ML libraries. AutoML compares candidate models, generates a notebook per trial you can edit, and is not built into ML Runtime 18.0 or above. Features: Feature Store recommends Feature Views for new work, while feature tables in Unity Catalog stay valid; the workspace feature store is legacy; offline tables serve training and batch scoring, online stores serve low-latency lookups. MLflow: log params, metrics and models, search runs and compare them in the UI. Registry: use Unity Catalog models with aliases such as Champion and tags, not stages; the workspace registry is legacy. Promote with aliases, and load with models:/catalog.schema.model@alias.

concepts.heading: Domain 2, Data Processing (19 percent)
concepts.body: Think of this domain as preparing features without distorting them. Summary statistics describe a column; outliers are flagged with standard deviations when the data is roughly symmetric, or with the IQR rule (below Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR) when it is skewed. Histograms show shape and skew, box plots show outliers, scatter plots and correlations compare features. Imputation replaces missing values with the mean or median for numeric columns (median is robust to outliers) or the mode or a constant for categories, and a fitted imputer must be reused on test data. One-hot encoding suits categories with few levels and no order; many levels explode the width, and tree models can cope with other encodings. A log transform tames right-skewed positive values; a model trained on a logged target returns logs, which must be exponentiated before reporting. Fit every transformer on training data only to avoid leakage.

concepts.heading: Domain 3, Model Development (31 percent)
concepts.body: Pick the algorithm from the target: regression for numbers, classification for classes. For imbalanced classes, accuracy misleads: with 5 positives per 1000 rows, always predicting negative scores 99.5 percent accuracy and finds nothing, so use precision, recall, F1 or area under the precision-recall curve and consider class weights or resampling. In Spark ML an estimator has fit and returns a transformer that has transform; a Pipeline chains stages so the same steps run at training and scoring. Tuning: random or Bayesian search with Optuna or Ray Tune is usually cheaper than an exhaustive grid for large spaces (open-source Hyperopt is legacy). Models in a grid: combinations times folds, so 12 combinations with 3 folds fit 36 models, while a train-validation split fits 12. Regression metrics: RMSE punishes large errors, MAE is robust, R squared is variance explained. Remember exp for log targets, and the U-shaped validation curve for complexity.

concepts.heading: Domain 4, Model Deployment (12 percent) and how to spend the hours
concepts.body: Weights are 38, 19, 31 and 12 percent of 48 scored questions, about 18, 9, 15 and 6 questions. Study order by weight: domain 1, then 3, then 2, then 4; the 31 percent of model development and 38 percent of Databricks ML together are 69 percent. Deployment is the smallest but is decided by a few rules. Mode: batch for stored results read later, real-time endpoint for a caller who waits, streaming for an endless feed scored in seconds to minutes. Custom models are logged with MLflow, registered in Unity Catalog and served from an endpoint. Batch scoring uses load_model with predict on one node and spark_udf at scale. Streaming scoring uses Structured Streaming with a checkpoint, and a model swap needs a full refresh. Query with dataframe_split, authenticate with M2M OAuth, and split traffic with traffic_percentage on one endpoint. When two answers fit, choose the one that solves the stated need with the least engineering.

examPoints: Weights from the exam guide: Databricks Machine Learning 38, Model Development 31, Data Processing 19, Model Deployment 12 percent of 48 scored questions. Review in that order.

Match the object to the situation: Feature Views or feature tables in Unity Catalog, Unity Catalog models with aliases instead of stages, deploy code over deploy models, Optuna or Ray Tune instead of Hyperopt, and a metric that fits imbalance (precision, recall, F1) rather than accuracy.

Read the stem for the deciding word: stored and read later is batch, a caller waits is a real-time endpoint, an endless feed is streaming; fits in memory is pandas, does not fit is spark_udf; log target and currency is exp.

quiz.q: When planning final review time, which order matches the weight of the exam domains from largest to smallest?
choices: Model Deployment, Data Processing, Model Development, then Databricks Machine Learning
Data Processing, Model Deployment, Databricks Machine Learning, then Model Development
Databricks Machine Learning, Model Development, Data Processing, Model Deployment
Model Development, Databricks Machine Learning, Model Deployment, then Data Processing
quiz.explain: The weights are 38 percent for Databricks Machine Learning, 31 for Model Development, 19 for Data Processing and 12 for Model Deployment, so that is the order in which review time pays off. The smallest domain should not come first.

quiz.q: A fraud model is evaluated on 1000 transactions of which 5 are fraudulent. A baseline that predicts not fraud for every row is proposed. How should the team judge candidates?
choices: Use precision and recall for fraud, because the baseline has 99.5 percent accuracy and finds none
Use accuracy alone, since the baseline already reaches 99.5 percent and further tuning is unnecessary
Use R squared on the predicted class labels, because a value near 1 would show that the model is useful
Use RMSE between the predicted labels and a log transform of the labels to reduce the class imbalance
quiz.explain: Always predicting the majority class gives 995 of 1000 correct, which is 99.5 percent accuracy with zero fraud found. Precision, recall, F1 or area under the precision-recall curve expose that. R squared and RMSE on labels do not address imbalance.

days.recap: Weights: D1 38, D3 31, D2 19, D4 12 percent. Databricks ML: deploy code, Feature Views or Unity Catalog feature tables, MLflow, Unity Catalog models with aliases, AutoML notebooks. Processing: IQR or standard deviation for outliers, median imputation, one-hot for low-cardinality categories, log for skew. Development: metric by imbalance, estimator to transformer pipelines, Optuna or Ray Tune, folds times combinations, exp for log targets, bias-variance. Deployment: batch, real-time or streaming by consumption, pandas or spark_udf, dataframe_split, traffic_percentage.
